Should You Invest Lump Sum or Invest Periodically? When you receive an inheritance or another large sum of money, have you ever wondered whether to invest it all at once, or spread the money out and invest it gradually? History over the past 150 years tells us that the North American stock market rises in about two out of every three years. From a statistical perspective, the longer your money stays in the market, the more likely it is to grow. Therefore, the solution to this dilemma is to invest lump sum, while maintaining the awareness that the market could fall at any time. If you are uneasy about investing lump sum, you can set up a simple system for incremental investing (for example, investing 25% of the total amount on the first day of every month, continuing this for four months).
While trillions of dollars are managed by Wall Street professionals who charge high management fees, it is usually the managers who reap massive profits, not the clients.
Don’t think you know more than the market; no one knows more than the market. Don’t act based on your own opinion; you think it’s just your idea, but in reality, millions of people think the same way.
The reason the power of compounding is so counterintuitive is that we rarely view time as an ally. Over time, everything around us seems to degrade and lose value. The top-tier computer bought a few years ago starts slowing down; the house requires expensive maintenance to withstand the elements; even our bodies age. In investing, the situation is exactly the opposite. Investing is one of the few areas where time is on our side.
Investing is frustrating because we always feel we could be doing better. If we invest during a market downturn, we will be disappointed when the market rises sharply because we didn’t invest more. If the market falls after we invest, we will regret it due to bad luck, saying we should have waited longer.
This emotion is widespread, and as investors, we need to recognize it. We can always do better, even if we are right, even if we achieve good returns—we can always do better. Investing is almost certainly going to be disappointing, at least in the short term.
If paying attention to the latest economic developments could make people rich, journalists would already be millionaires. Dear reader, let me tell you a secret: journalists are not millionaires!
News applications aim to draw you into their echo chamber from your phone’s home screen, allowing them to display ads and monitor your behavior. For you, the news is not important information; it is bait that pulls you out of your life and traps you. Turn it off.
In my opinion, the most insidious articles are those that explain why a certain company’s stock rose or fell. These articles are titled things like, “Bank of America Stock Falls Today, Here’s Why,” or “Three Reasons Why Netflix Stock Plunged.” The tone of these articles often makes us think that the author knew the decline was coming and graciously typed out an explanation for us—a small miracle. This makes people even more convinced that predicting a decline is possible. In fact, the authors of these articles don’t know the stock movement; they are merely being “after-the-fact Zhuge Liang” (a reference to a brilliant strategist who often appears after the event), doing so to attract investor clicks.
What smart investors do is forget what might happen and prepare for possibilities through diversification, rational asset allocation, and patience.
In the short term, the stock market is like cocaine—never let it affect you. In most cases, company profits grow over time, and that is the key. What is important is the systematic nature of the investment. Therefore, becoming a good investor requires extreme self-discipline.
In my line of work, the money earned from selling advice is more than the money earned from following it. This is one of the conditions for the magazine industry to survive, the other being the reader’s short memory.
Warren Buffett once said that even if epoch-making disasters like war or pandemics occur, we should not stop investing. In a letter to shareholders, he recounted how his 11-year-old self bought his first batch of stocks on March 11, 1942, three months after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
In the three days before Buffett bought his first stock, the headline of The New York Times was “Japanese Forces Break Through Malayan Defenses.” The next day, the paper announced: “Japanese Forces Invade New Guinea from Two Points, Occupy Yangon, and Advance on the Western Front of Burma.” The news on the third day was: “Enemy Artillery Approaches Australia, 98,000 Surrendered in Java, Reportedly.”
Times are always uncertain; violent events constantly threaten world peace, and the risk of economic recession and depression always accompanies us. Here is a brief summary of negative events over the past decade:
Russia and Ukraine launched a large-scale conflict, resulting in thousands of deaths. Severe riots occurred at the Capitol Building in Washington D.C. The COVID-19 pandemic caused millions of deaths, leading to a stock market crash and global economic recession. Rebel armed groups attacked oil refineries in Saudi Arabia. Long-term optimists predict that the world collapses about once every decade.
A stock market crash is like lightning; it can leave even the most rational people stunned. However, just as lightning ushered in the electric age, a stock market crash should be welcomed by most of us.
Many people think they can handle a stock market crash without panicking. But a stock market crash is not just a notification popping up on a phone screen. We calculate our losses in our minds, which might be equivalent to several months or even years of our salary. Only then do we feel genuine panic.
The S&P 500 index averages three drops of 5% or more per year.
Over the past 100 years, the S&P 500 index has experienced a 10% drop approximately every 16 months. Over the last century, a 20% drop occurs on average every seven years. Since the 1950s, the S&P 500 index has also experienced three drops of about 50%, averaging once every 22 years. This famous “market volatility” is so common that we shouldn’t be surprised by it, yet it always surprises us!
The losses caused by downturns are usually temporary. For example, since World War II, the market has averaged only four months to recover from a maximum 20% drop and return to its previous level.
Market returns are never free; they never will be in the future either.
A market adjustment is not a flaw in the financial system. Accepting that investing involves losses is the price you pay for long-term growth. No adjustment, no risk; no risk, no reward.
Setting new highs is the norm, not the exception, in the stock market. Therefore, if you delay investing because the market is strong or at a new high, you might be delaying for a long time!
Since 1928, the S&P 500 index has set a new historical high, on average, every 20 trading days.
From 1926 to 2019, the S&P 500 index rose for nearly three out of every four years. What about the year after a bull market? The index still rises…
After astonishing and absurd surges, such as when the index rises by 50% in 12 months, it should obviously pull back, right? But that’s not the case. Historically, after an incredible year of gains, the market’s return in the second year is indeed negative, with an average return of -1.5%. But after that year of 50% gains, the average market return three years later is 42%, and five years later, it is 66%, not including dividend payments.
If investing were easy, everyone would be rich. Investing shouldn’t be easy; those who think it is easy are fools.

The stock market is like a very excited dog, which is tied to one end of a long leash. The owner holds the leash, and the dog sniffs randomly in all directions. Assuming in this example, the dog owner represents the economy, and he is walking in New York City, starting from the Columbus Circle, passing through Central Park, and arriving at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. From one second to the next, the dog might turn right or left; its movement cannot be precisely predicted.
However, in the long run, the dog’s direction of movement is not mysterious; just like the owner, this dog is moving northeast at a speed of approximately 3 miles per hour.
Surprisingly, almost all people tracking the market are focusing on the dog, rather than the dog owner.

content: On Saving and Thrifty Lifestyle The Power of High Savings Save and invest an unwavering 50% of your income. The beauty of a high savings rate is twofold: you learn to live on less, even as you have more to invest. When you can live on 4% of your investments per year, you are financially independent. Financial Independence vs. Dependence If your lifestyle matches or exceeds your income, you are a slave. It’s better to adapt yourself and your attitudes to the numbers than to adapt the strategies to your psychological comfort levels. Long-Term Savings Strategy If financial independence is your goal, your savings rate in these years should be high. As you invest that money each month, it serves to smooth out the market’s volatility. Be persistent. Life is uncertain. On the Stock Market and Investing Fundamental Investment Rules Rule #1: Never lose money. Rule #2: Never forget rule #1. The Stock Market as a Wealth-Building Tool The stock market is a powerful wealth-building tool, and you should be investing in it. Embrace indexing. Crashes, pullbacks, and corrections are all absolutely normal. Avoiding Short-Term Speculation Any investing done short-term is, by definition, speculation. Market timing is an unwinnable game over time. To play this market-timing game well even once, you need to be right twice: first, you need to call the high, and then, you need to call the low. Market Dynamics and Long-Term Perspective The market always recovers. Always. Everybody makes money when the market is rising. But what determines whether it will make you wealthy or leave you bleeding on the side of the road is what you do during the times it is collapsing. Common Pitfalls in the Stock Market Most people lose money in the stock market. Here’s why: We think we can time the market. We believe we can pick individual stocks. We believe we can pick winning mutual fund managers. Dollar-Cost Averaging By dollar-cost averaging, you are betting that the market will drop, saving yourself some pain. For any given year, the odds of this happening are only about 23%. But the market is about 77% more likely to rise, in which case you will have spared yourself some gain. With each new invested portion, you’ll be paying more for your shares. Put all your eggs in one basket and forget about it.
summary:
On Saving and Thrifty Lifestyle

The Power of High Savings

  • Save and invest an unwavering 50% of your income.
  • The beauty of a high savings rate is twofold: you learn to live on less, even as you have more to invest.
  • When you can live on 4% of your investments per year, you are financially independent.

Financial Independence vs. Dependence

  • If your lifestyle matches or exceeds your income, you are a slave.
  • It’s better to adapt yourself and your attitudes to the numbers than to adapt the strategies to your psychological comfort levels.

Long-Term Savings Strategy

  • If financial independence is your goal, your savings rate in these years should be high. As you invest that money each month, it serves to smooth out the market’s volatility.
  • Be persistent. Life is uncertain.

On the Stock Market and Investing

Fundamental Investment Rules

  • Rule #1: Never lose money.
  • Rule #2: Never forget rule #1.

The Stock Market as a Wealth-Building Tool

  • The stock market is a powerful wealth-building tool, and you should be investing in it.
  • Embrace indexing.
  • Crashes, pullbacks, and corrections are all absolutely normal.

Avoiding Short-Term Speculation

  • Any investing done short-term is, by definition, speculation.
  • Market timing is an unwinnable game over time. To play this market-timing game well even once, you need to be right twice: first, you need to call the high, and then, you need to call the low.

Market Dynamics and Long-Term Perspective

  • The market always recovers. Always.
  • Everybody makes money when the market is rising. But what determines whether it will make you wealthy or leave you bleeding on the side of the road is what you do during the times it is collapsing.

Common Pitfalls in the Stock Market

  • Most people lose money in the stock market. Here’s why:
    1. We think we can time the market.
    2. We believe we can pick individual stocks.
    3. We believe we can pick winning mutual fund managers.

Dollar-Cost Averaging

  • By dollar-cost averaging, you are betting that the market will drop, saving yourself some pain. For any given year, the odds of this happening are only about 23%. But the market is about 77% more likely to rise, in which case you will have spared yourself some gain. With each new invested portion, you’ll be paying more for your shares.
  • Put all your eggs in one basket and forget about it.
title: Achieving Financial Independence Through Savings and Investing

Date Calculation Today is April 20th, so 14 days later is the 34th, which means 34 minus 30—May 4th. Because 20 plus 14 equals 34, the date would be April 34th. And April 34th is equal to May 4th, that’s all (Figure 2.6). She invented a non-existent date just to make her derivation lead directly to the target. And this in no way hindered her from getting the correct result! Complex numbers are just like that—they arrive unexpectedly.
Fearless of Being Different Do not fear being different; that is the wisdom of the umbrella. Let us be fearless, neither feeling ashamed nor holding prejudices. Once we accept the abstract umbrella held above our heads and enter the world of mathematics, we no longer have to rely entirely on reality. You don’t have to trap yourself in useless limitations or embarrassing preconceived notions. Do you want an April 34th? Take it! Do you want a negative number? Take it! Do you want infinity? Take it! If all these ideas do not interfere with your organization of thought, but even help it, then why deprive yourself of them? You are free!
Mathematics and Imagination Studying mathematics is creating an imaginative world where our thoughts can wander freely, without worrying about the constraints of reality. Although this way of thinking covers a much wider scope, it is very similar to the way the Nippurians used to simplify multiplication in the world of addition. When you encounter a scientific problem, the following method is often very effective:
Create a mathematical world where you can model the problem; Solve the problem within that mathematical world; Transfer the result back into the real world.

Trump’s New Tariff Policy and Stock Market Plunge After Trump announced the latest tariff policy, the global stock market plummeted. So far this year, the market has lost 20%. While I am not panicked, this experience has made me deeply understand one principle: a certain amount of cash must be held in the investment portfolio.
Unexpected Market Events Always Arrive The market always experiences various unexpected events, once every few years. For example, the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 market crash, the 2020 Wuhan outbreak, and even the 2025 economic world war. Every market crash is a perfect buying opportunity. The market is filled with cheap assets, and if you don’t have cash, you might miss the chance to get rich.
The Importance of Holding Cash When the market is running well, the cash in hand can make you feel very uncomfortable, because you are watching the profits slip away from you. However, if you have enough composure, this cash can bring you greater returns in the future. This is the important reason why you must allocate cash in the investment portfolio. Of course, there is also a less important reason: when you need cash, you don’t have to be forced to sell assets.
You might be thinking, why hold cash when the market is good? After all, watching others make money while you are doing nothing—that feeling is indeed unpleasant. But please remember, market volatility is normal, and cash allows you to seize opportunities at critical moments. More importantly, it brings you inner peace and security. 😚

Comparison between the Animal World and the Human World In the animal world, the strong consume the bodies of the weak; in the human world, the strong consume the resources of the weak. Once you fail economically, your entire life will collapse—this society is an upgraded version of the animal world.
The Metaphor of the Wolf and the Sheep Does the wolf want to eat the sheep because the sheep did something wrong? No, it is because the wolf is hungry. The wolf ate the sheep, and when the sheep grew old and could barely walk, it was killed by a younger wolf. The sheep, upon seeing this, happily said, “Justice may be late, but it will never be absent.”
The Sheep’s Misunderstanding But the sheep simply doesn’t know that no matter how much the wolves bite each other, their attitude toward the sheep remains consistent. For those qualified to reach the dining table, they can compete with each other, or they can cooperate with each other.
Cooperation and Competition Among the Strong But for those outside who are not qualified to reach the dining table, they can immediately set aside their prejudices and fight together to seize the prey. Because what they care about is not whether this sheep should be eaten, but who will eat it.

There are just three primary reasons for which you should consider selling your stocks:
1. Investment Reasons No Longer Exist For example, Blockbuster was a great company for many years and was well ahead of the curve when it came to in-home DVD rentals. However, they didn’t adapt to the streaming revolution. In fact, Blockbuster turned down the chance to buy Netflix on three separate occasions.
2. Compromised Management Small lies eventually lead to bigger lies. If you begin to spot inconsistencies in the way management communicates its shortcomings or if it starts to treat everyone else like a bunch of dunces, it is likely that the management is incompetent. You’re best served by getting out quickly.
3. Better Opportunities Sometimes, better investment opportunities arise, and it makes sense to reallocate your capital to take advantage of them.
Remember to Keep the Following Investment Principles The Warren Buffett Test: Buy great businesses at fair prices. See if you can describe the business to a 10-year-old. Understand the True Business: How well do you know what drives the profits of the business? Founder Syndrome: How honest and reliable is management? Is there a succession plan in place, or does it all depend on the founder? Intangible Assets: Does the company have any brand loyalty? Does it have intellectual property like patents or trademarks? These are things that don’t show up on a balance sheet. Management Quality: How well does management align the business with the economics of the industry? How well do they reinvest capital? Sales and Marketing: How dedicated is the company to sales and marketing? What is the quality of their teams? How are their key metrics looking year-to-year? Long-Term Focus: Is management focused on short-term metrics, or does it invest resources for the long run? Moat: A moat is a phenomenon that gives a company an unfair advantage in its field. It could be brand loyalty, a superior supply chain, sheer size, etc. Can It Weather a Storm?: How well will the business perform under a stress test?

The Secret to Successful Investing What is the secret to successful investing? It is to do nothing—well, not quite nothing, but our point is that to be successful, you need to limit your activity as much as possible when it comes to managing your investments.
The Risks of Short-Term Trading Short-term trading involves all kinds of risks. Essentially, a trader is attempting to gauge how the market feels about a stock. Here’s an experiment for you to conduct: walk over to your partner and try to guess how they’re feeling about something. You might be able to guess what is wrong some of the time, but not all the time. This is similar to trying to predict the market’s sentiment.
The Power of Buy and Hold The most intelligent investment decision you can make is to buy and hold stocks for as long as possible. Leave the constant jumping in and out to the traders and other speculators. Resist everything that can potentially cause you to exit early or trade too much in a single stock.
If you don’t have the cash to pay your bills, you’re going to be tempted to sell some of your investments before they have a chance to blossom fully.
Essential Savings Priorities Your Rainy Day Fund: 3-6 months’ worth of living expenses that you’ve saved up in case you or your partner lose your jobs. Readily Accessible Cash: This money should not be invested under any circumstances. Your rainy day fund should be held in readily accessible cash. Tuition Payments: Money that is needed to pay bills or your child’s tuition should not be invested in the markets. Down Payments: Even if you’re planning on purchasing a home several years down the road, don’t rely on the stock market to generate enough money for a down payment.

Stock Market Trading Pre-Checklist I. General Principles (Must Read Before Every Trade) Goal Confirmation
Does my trade serve my long-term investment goals? Am I trading impulsively due to short-term market fluctuations, emotions, or external advice? (If “Yes,” pause and calmly review the situation) Cost Awareness
Do transaction fees (commission, stamp duty, management fees) significantly impact the return? Is “friction cost” accumulating due to frequent trading? Discipline
Does the trade adhere to the pre-set strategy (e.g., DCA plan, rebalancing rules)? Is there a “regret mindset” (e.g., annoyance over not acting in time)? II. ETF Purchase Pre-Checklist 1. Basic Conditions Is the long-term holding period ≥ 3-5 years? (Conflicts with the concept of short-term trading vs. passive investment) Is the tracked index clear (e.g., S&P 500, CSI 300) and sufficiently liquid? (Avoid niche or complex derivatives) Are the fee rates reasonable (e.g., annual fee ≤ 0.3%)? (Low cost is a core advantage of passive investment) 2. Market and Valuation Is the current market in a state of extreme overvaluation? (Refer to PE/PB quantiles: Caution is needed if the S&P 500 PE is above the 25th percentile) Am I blindly following the trend due to recent gains? (Beware of the “this time is different” cognitive trap) 3. Risk Management Is the portfolio overly concentrated in a single industry or region? (e.g., Tech stocks exceeding 40%, requiring diversification) Have I reserved enough cash to handle Black Swan events? (e.g., If emergency reserves are insufficient, postpone adding more) 4. Emotional Test Is the reason for buying based on rational analysis, rather than “Fear of Missing Out” (FOMO)? Am I buying at a low price due to panic selling? (When the market crashes, assess calmly, don’t just blindly buy) III. ETF Sale Pre-Checklist 1. Core Principles Is there a clear, non-negotiable reason to sell? (Passive investment prioritizes “holding”; selling must be deliberate) Am I selling in a panic due to short-term volatility (e.g., 20% drawdown within 1 year)? (Historical data shows short-term drawdowns usually recover) 2. Necessity Assessment Has the index component significantly deviated from the target (e.g., one company in a Tech ETF has excessive weight)? Has the goal been achieved (e.g., the education fund has accumulated the required capital)? 3. Risk and Alternatives Does the capital have a clear destination with higher potential returns after selling? (e.g., shifting to bonds or cash, requiring opportunity cost assessment) Am I “cutting losses and exiting” due to a market crash? (Historical experience shows exiting at a low point often misses the recovery) 4. Emotion and Discipline Am I trading based on media-driven panic sentiment? (e.g., “Doomsday” or “Bull Market End” narratives require calm verification) Have I violated the pre-set selling rules (e.g., take-profit line or stop-loss line)? (Undisciplined selling easily undermines the long-term strategy) IV. Rebalancing Operation Checklist 1. Trigger Conditions Has the preset time interval been reached (e.g., quarterly/annually)? (To avoid excessive adjustments) Has the asset allocation deviated from the target ratio by more than ±5%-10%? (e.g., Stock allocation should be 60%, but is currently 70%) 2. Cost and Efficiency Will the rebalancing lead to high costs (e.g., frequent trading fees, taxes)? Am I prioritizing using new capital for adjustment rather than selling existing holdings? (e.g., using new funds to top up under-allocated assets during DCA) 3. Market Judgment Am I adjusting due to extreme market valuation (e.g., Tech stocks are overvalued, shifting to value stocks)? (Requires caution to avoid the “market timing selection” trap) Am I adjusting the strategic allocation due to long-term trend changes (e.g., energy transition)? (Requires combining fundamental research, not just short-term volatility) 4. Discipline Does the operation align with the “Buy Low, Sell High” logic of rebalancing? (e.g., selling over-allocated assets when they are overvalued, and buying under-allocated assets when they are undervalued) V. Post-Operation Record (Mandatory After Every Execution) Operation Type: Buy / Sell / Rebalance Decision Basis: List the key points marked “Yes” in the checklist Market Environment: Current PE/PB, Interest Rates, Economic Cycle Stage Emotional Score: 1-10 (1 = Extreme Panic, 10 = Extreme Greed) Review Marker: Record the outcome after 3 months and confirm if it met expectations VI. Ultimate Question (Muttered Before Every Trade) “In 10 years, will this decision make me richer or will it make me regret it more?” “If I couldn’t trade for the next year, would my current operation still be rational?” If a trade cannot withstand the test of a year-long pause, it is highly likely to harm long-term returns.
By following this systematic process, you can reduce emotional interference and avoid common mistakes (such as chasing highs and selling lows, or over-trading), ultimately achieving stable compound growth through a passive investment strategy. Wishing you successful investing!

Ultimately, it still comes down to that famous saying: The market is a voting machine in the short term, and a weighing machine in the long term.
Speculation is a 0 and a Game - My Lessons in Speculation
The Essence of Reducing Trading Frequency
Investment vs. Speculation in “Enough”
Market Sentiment is Random The market is essentially like a person of average intelligence. You might occasionally guess the market’s sentiment, but to make money, you need to guess correctly twice (the buying point + the selling point). And if you guess wrong just once, you will lose money. This is a very simple mathematical problem.
Some Forces Want You to Trade Short-Term There are always stories that make you want to trade short-term for quick money. This is similar to seeing news about a major jackpot—it is essentially an advertisement. This is because securities companies, exchanges, and tax bureaus all like you to trade frequently and repeatedly. They are leveraging the greed in your nature to entice you into these speculative operations.
Never Make Investment Decisions During Strong Emotions Never make investment decisions when you are experiencing strong emotions. Whether that emotion is fear, excitement, sadness, or greed and impulse, they act like a fog obscuring rational judgment.
When the market crashes sharply, the fear fueled by adrenaline might cause you to sell quality assets at a bargain price; When the bull market is rampant, the euphoria driven by dopamine easily tempts you to buy at high prices. Even sudden sad events in life can act like an invisible filter, distorting your perception of the risk-reward ratio. True investment wisdom lies in establishing a decision-making mechanism that is insulated from emotional fluctuations—replacing ad-hoc judgment with pre-set trading discipline, and hedging against human weaknesses with data-supported valuation models. Reflection on Consumption and Demand If you analyze consumption closely, it is actually about enjoying the feeling of buying and owning at that moment. “Demand” is imagined. Ladies, do you really need so many shoes, so many clothes? Gentlemen, do you really need so many electronic devices? Take a close look—how many things in your home haven’t been touched in over ten years?
Advice for Short-Term Investing Advice: “If you love short-term investing, it is best to start when you are very poor.” Anyway, you will lose your principal, because you are poor, so you won’t lose too much, but you can accumulate very good experience.
Factors Determining Investment Commodity Prices Whether the price of an investment commodity will rise in the future depends on whether the owner will be significantly richer in the future than they are now, especially for those who must own this investment commodity in the future—that is, the group with inelastic demand—whether they will be richer than they are now.
Investment Strategy Following the Youth All you have to do is follow the youth. You can observe the smartest young people of this generation, those whose future income growth is the fastest. Where are they going, what are they doing? What inelastic demand will they have in the future? Go to where they are going in the future and buy the assets. When these young people arrive, the asset prices will rise.
Spend Today’s Money or Tomorrow’s Money? Whether to spend today’s money or tomorrow’s money, the best judgment is to compare today’s income with future income. If you feel that income growth will exceed 10%, but the investment return rate is only 5%, you should spend today’s money without saving it. If you feel that future income growth will be lower than the investment return rate, you should honestly save money, saving and investing as much as possible.
The Importance of Investment Return Rate Your investment return rate must exceed the income growth rate of your demographic. Only then is it a good investment; otherwise, it is actually a depreciating investment, and you might as well spend it directly on consumption.
The Lesson of Detroit Real Estate Investment In Detroit, USA, if you bought property there in the 1950s, you would find that no matter how you bought it, you could make money, because a continuous stream of workers poured in, and American-produced cars were sold all over the world, and all the money from America flowed into Detroit. However, if you still hold Detroit property after the 1980s, no matter how smart you are, your money will become less and less, because the industry declined, and the population is leaving.
Strategy for Middle-Aged and Elderly Investors Middle-aged and elderly investors must not only focus on what the people around them are investing in. They must also look at what the youth are preparing to invest in, because the youth are the hope of the future.
The Best Time for Real Estate Investment The best time to buy a house is after the property price has risen a bit from the bottom. It doesn’t need to rise much, maybe around 5%. Wait until the market trend is basically established, and then go in and buy.
The Core Secret of Stable Real Estate Investment The second core secret of stable real estate investment is maintaining positive cash flow, which is often the dilemma that investors always face.

content: 1. Basic Concepts of Rebalancing Asset Allocation: Investors set the proportion of different asset classes (e.g., stocks, bonds, cash) based on their risk tolerance and return goals. Market Fluctuation: Market fluctuations can cause asset proportions to deviate from the target (e.g., a rise in stocks might make their share in the portfolio too high). Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio back to the target proportion by buying and selling assets. 2. Methods of Rebalancing Time-based Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio at fixed time intervals (e.g., quarterly or annually). Ratio-based Rebalancing: Adjusting when a specific asset class deviates from the target proportion by more than a certain threshold (e.g., 5%). 3. Advantages of Rebalancing Risk Control: Prevents a single asset from having too high a proportion, thereby reducing risk. Discipline: Avoids emotional trading, maintaining the stability of the investment strategy. Return Optimization: May enhance long-term returns by buying low and selling high. 4. Disadvantages of Rebalancing Transaction Costs: Frequent adjustments may increase trading fees. Tax Implications: In taxable accounts, rebalancing may generate capital gains tax. Market Trends: In a unidirectional market (trend), rebalancing may reduce returns. 5. Implementation of Rebalancing Determine Target Proportion: Setting asset allocation based on risk preference. Monitor Portfolio: Regularly checking asset proportions. Execute Adjustment: Restoring the target proportion by buying and selling assets. Summary Rebalancing is a tool for “exchanging short-term transaction costs for long-term risk control.” It is suitable for volatile or sector-rotating markets, but may incur opportunity costs in unidirectional trend markets. When executing, it is recommended to combine threshold rules (e.g., rebalancing after a 10% deviation) rather than mechanically operating based on time. Furthermore, it is recommended to operate a maximum of twice a year.

  • Market Fluctuation: Market fluctuations can cause asset proportions to deviate from the target (e.g., a rise in stocks might make their share in the portfolio too high).
  • Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio back to the target proportion by buying and selling assets.

2. Methods of Rebalancing

  • Time-based Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio at fixed time intervals (e.g., quarterly or annually).
  • Ratio-based Rebalancing: Adjusting when a specific asset class deviates from the target proportion by more than a certain threshold (e.g., 5%).

3. Advantages of Rebalancing

  • Risk Control: Prevents a single asset from having too high a proportion, thereby reducing risk.
  • Discipline: Avoids emotional trading, maintaining the stability of the investment strategy.
  • Return Optimization: May enhance long-term returns by buying low and selling high.

4. Disadvantages of Rebalancing

  • Transaction Costs: Frequent adjustments may increase trading fees.
  • Tax Implications: In taxable accounts, rebalancing may generate capital gains tax.
  • Market Trends: In a unidirectional market (trend), rebalancing may reduce returns.

5. Implementation of Rebalancing

  • Determine Target Proportion: Setting asset allocation based on risk preference.
  • Monitor Portfolio: Regularly checking asset proportions.
  • Execute Adjustment: Restoring the target proportion by buying and selling assets.

When executing, it is recommended to combine threshold rules (e.g., rebalancing after a 10% deviation) rather than mechanically operating based on time. Furthermore, it is recommended to operate a maximum of twice a year.
title: Rebalancing between aggressive and defensive stocks

content:
To Be a Winner, or to Avoid Being a Loser? Being proactive can yield greater rewards, but in the long run, it is not always beneficial. When luck is bad, you may encounter developments that are less than expected, leading to frustration. Short-term success is generally recognized, but there is insufficient attention paid to its persistence and stability in the records. Timing of Offensive and Defensive Shifts Few people (if any) have the ability to instantly adjust tactics to match market conditions, so investors should stick to one method, hoping that this method can apply to various different situations.
They might adopt an aggressive strategy, hoping to earn a lot when investments succeed and recoup costs when they fail; or they might emphasize a defensive strategy, hoping to match market performance during a bull market and lose less than others during a bear market.
We cannot determine the exact timing for offense and defense So, we can only choose based on our own conditions. The safety of your asset portfolio should be determined by how much potential return you are willing to sacrifice. There is no correct answer, only a trade-off.
Offense An aggressive tactic raises potential highs and lowers potential lows. However, if you exclusively use an offensive investment approach, when things go wrong, it might prevent you from recovering. On the other hand, defensive investment can help you navigate difficult periods, giving you enough time to enjoy the ultimate returns brought by smart investing.
Defense Defensive investment has two main elements. The first is eliminating underperforming assets from the portfolio. To achieve this, the best approach is to conduct in-depth evaluations, adopt high stock selection standards, demand low prices, and set a relatively large margin of error (which will be mentioned later in this chapter). Furthermore, do not bet on uncertain scenarios such as continuous bullish trends or beautiful forecasts and developments.
The second element is avoiding market bear markets, especially avoiding the risk of an imminent crash. In addition to excluding individual underperforming assets from the portfolio (as mentioned earlier), defensive investment also requires thoughtful asset diversification, limiting overall risk exposure, and focusing on safety.
summary:
To Be a Winner, or to Avoid Being a Loser?

  1. Being proactive can yield greater rewards, but in the long run, it is not always beneficial.
  2. When luck is bad, you may encounter developments that are less than expected, leading to frustration.
  3. Short-term success is generally recognized, but there is insufficient attention paid to its persistence and stability in the records.

Timing of Offensive and Defensive Shifts

Few people (if any) have the ability to instantly adjust tactics to match market conditions, so investors should stick to one method, hoping that this method can apply to various different situations.
title: The timing of the investor's shift from offense to defense (or defensive to offensive)

content: We should spend time trying to find value in knowable factors such as industries, companies, and securities, rather than making decisions based on our predictions about the relatively unknowable overall economic world and market trends. Because we cannot know the exact shape of the future, we must acquire value through methods such as firm conviction, views derived from future analysis, and buying in at a lower price when opportunities arise. We must adopt defensive investing because many outcomes may be unfavorable to us. More importantly, we must confirm the ability to survive in the market under negative outcomes, rather than guaranteeing maximum returns under favorable outcomes. To increase the chances of success, when extreme situations occur, we must emphasize that the actions taken should be contrary to the crowd: being aggressive when the market is sluggish, and being cautious when the market is euphoric. Because the results are inherently highly uncertain, unless they have been verified through many experiments, we must view the decisions and the resulting outcomes with a skeptical perspective—whether they are good outcomes or bad outcomes.

content:
Our world undergoes cyclical changes, primarily because of human involvement. Mechanical things can develop linearly, and time can continuously move forward, allowing machines with sufficient momentum to constantly progress. However, for fields like history and economics to advance, they rely on humans. When humans are involved, change and cyclical replacement occur. I believe the main reason is that ordinary people possess emotions, are volatile, and are neither steadfast nor objective.
Principle One: Most things follow cycles. Principle Two: The greatest opportunities for profit and loss arise when others forget Principle One. When ordinary people feel that things are progressing well and are optimistic about the future, their behavior is greatly influenced. They spend more and save less. They borrow money for enjoyment, or they borrow money to increase potential profits, even if this makes their financial situation less stable (of course, when optimistic, investors forget the concept of “instability”). Furthermore, they are willing to pay more for current value or for a portion of the future.
Periodically, when upward and downward trends have continued for a long time, and reach an extreme (or extremes), people start saying, “This time is different.” They cite changes in geopolitics, institutions, technology, or behavior, believing that this has rendered the “old rules” ineffective. They infer recent trends and make investment decisions. However, the results show that the old rules are still valid, and the cycle restarts. Ultimately, trees do not pierce the sky straight up, and few things’ values drop to zero; most phenomena undergo cyclical changes.
Our conclusion is that for the majority of the time, the future looks very similar to the past, featuring both upward cycles and downward cycles. The best time to say things will improve is when the market is declining, and everyone is eager to sell things at extremely cheap prices. Conversely, when the market reaches a new high level and people propose positive rationalizations that have never been proven in the past, that is when danger lies. This has happened in the past, and it will happen again in the future.
summary: Our world undergoes cyclical changes, primarily because of human involvement. Mechanical things can develop linearly, and time can continuously move forward, allowing machines with sufficient momentum to constantly progress. However, for fields like history and economics to advance, they rely on humans. When humans are involved, change and cyclical replacement occur. I believe the main reason is that ordinary people possess emotions, are volatile, and are neither steadfast nor objective.
title: Law of Cycles: The Cyclical Nature of Markets and Human Behavior

content:
The desire to earn more, the fear of missing out on opportunities, the personality trait of comparing oneself to others, the influence of the group, and the dream of successful investment—these factors are almost universally present. Consequently, they exert a profound collective influence on most investors and the market, resulting in errors. These errors are frequent, widespread, and tend to repeat themselves.
Seven Mindsets Leading to Errors in Decision-Making Many people possess the intelligence to analyze data, but few are able to observe things deeply and withstand the powerful influence of psychological factors. In other words, many people arrive at similar conclusions based on their own analysis and cognition, but they act in drastically different ways due to varying psychological influences. The biggest investment bias does not come from information or analysis, but from mindset.
Greed Greed is defined as “an excessive or exhaustive desire, and usually a reprehensible possessiveness, especially for wealth or profit.”
Greed is an extremely powerful force. Its power is so great that it can override common sense, risk aversion, caution, logic, the memory of past painful lessons, determination, panic, and other elements that would normally make an investor avoid trouble. Furthermore, greed occasionally leads investors to join the pursuit of profit, only to pay the price in the end.
Fear Fear, like greed, implies excess. Therefore, fear is more akin to panic. Fear is an excessive worry that causes investors to remain inactive when they should be taking positive action.
Self-Deception Nothing is easier to self-deceive than oneself, because everyone, as long as they wish to, will believe it is true. Investors are always looking for a panacea, calling it the “Holy Grail” or the “Free Lunch,” but everyone wants a ticket that turns them into a wealthy person without taking any risks. Few question whether this ticket exists, or why they should receive it. Most importantly, the average person always maintains hope.
What factors make people believe in a panacea?
First, there is usually a factual basis for it. Then, a set of seemingly intelligent theories is fabricated, which the believers promote everywhere to persuade others. Subsequently, this theory accidentally generates profits, either because the theory has some value or simply because new believers join and drive up the price of the target asset. Finally, it appears to be a definite way to acquire wealth, and this creates a craze. Herd Mentality (Conformity) Not even when one insists on their own opinion, even if the crowd’s view is clearly absurd. Time and time again, the pressure of the herd and the desire to get rich cause people to abandon independent judgment and skepticism, suppressing their innate risk-averse mindset to believe in the unreasonable. Since this situation occurs so regularly, something must be at work, rather than merely random influence.
Envy Even if the force of greed is negative, it at least motivates others to strive for more profit. But the negative influence of comparing oneself to others is even stronger. This is what we consider the most dangerous trait of human nature.
A person who might be happy when isolated can feel miserable when they see others doing better. In the investment world, you will find that most investors find it difficult to sit idly by and watch others earn more money than them.
Hubris (Overconfidence) It is an enormous challenge to remain objective and prudent when facing the following realities:
We evaluate and compare short-term investment performance. During a bull market, making an inappropriate, even reckless, decision to increase risk often yields the best returns (and most of the time, it is a bull market). The best returns bring the greatest reward. When things go right, feeling smart and having others agree with it is a very pleasant feeling. In contrast, a thoughtful investor works diligently, earning stable returns during a bull market and losing less than others during a bear market. They avoid high-risk behavior because they know there is much they do not understand, and they suppress their hubris. In my view, this is the best formula for long-term wealth creation, but it does not satisfy the mindset in the short term. Emphasizing humility, caution, and risk control is not a glamorous path, and of course, investment should not seek glamour, but that is what people often think.
Surrender Mentality This is an investment behavior that is consistently observed in the later stages of a cycle. Investors try their best to stick to their beliefs, but when they cannot resist economic or psychological pressure, they surrender and follow the trend. Often, asset prices are too high and continue to rise, or the price is too low and continues to fall. Eventually, these trends shake the investor’s mindset, beliefs, and determination. Others profit because you refuse to buy a stock, while the stock you choose to buy hovers at a low price every day. Furthermore, the investment concept you originally thought was unsafe and unwise seems to be going in the right direction—selling the overpriced stock and buying the underpriced stock—but the investor does not do it. The tendency toward self-doubt, mixed with news of others’ success, forms a powerful force that leads the investor to make the wrong decision. And when this trend continues for a longer period, the force becomes stronger—this is another influence factor we must fight against.
summary: The desire to earn more, the fear of missing out on opportunities, the personality trait of comparing oneself to others, the influence of the group, and the dream of successful investment—these factors are almost universally present. Consequently, they exert a profound collective influence on most investors and the market, resulting in errors. These errors are frequent, widespread, and tend to repeat themselves.
title: The negative impact of confronting emotions

content:
Especially during a bull market, you often hear many people say: “High-risk investments bring higher returns. If you want to make more money, you must take on higher risks.” In fact, it is not possible to generate high returns solely through high-risk investments. Why? The answer is simple: If high-risk investments could reliably create high returns, then their risk wouldn’t be high!
The correct way to put it is that, in order to attract capital, high-risk investments must offer higher potential returns, higher guaranteed returns, or higher expected returns, but this absolutely does not mean that the higher potential return will always be realized.
Risk only exists in the future, and we cannot know exactly what the future will hold… When we look back at the past, the facts are clearly evident—we know that something happened. However, this certainty does not mean that the process that produced the result was clear and reliable. In every past situation, many things could have happened. But because only one thing happened, we tend to underestimate the existence of variability. When deciding whether or not to take on risk, I first assume that the normal situation will repeat itself. Although the normal situation does indeed repeat itself most of the time, sometimes something very different happens… Occasionally, rare things happen. Our predictions usually revolve around historical norms, at most making small adjustments… The key point is that most people typically predict the future will be similar to the past, and they underestimate the possibility of change. We have heard many predictions about the “worst-case scenario,” but the results are often even worse. Let me tell you about my father’s story. He was a habitual gambler, and one day he heard about a horse race with only one horse running, so he bet his rent money. However, halfway through the race, the horse jumped the rail and ran away. Things always tend to become worse than the average person expects. Perhaps “worst-case scenario” means “the worst case we have seen so far,” but it doesn’t mean it is the worst case of the future. The situation in 2007 was far worse than many people assumed for the worst-case scenario. Risk changes. If we say there is a “2% mortgage default rate” every year, even if the average figure over many years is indeed that, there is still a possibility that an abnormal amount of defaults will occur at some point, dragging down the performance of structured financial products. Some investors, especially those using high leverage, cannot get through this difficult time. People tend to overestimate their ability to measure risk, and they also overestimate their understanding of investment mechanisms they have never seen before. Theoretically, what makes humans different from other species is that we can point out something is dangerous without personally experiencing it. We don’t need to burn ourselves to know not to sit on the stove. However, during a bull market, this mechanism often fails to operate. People don’t first understand the risk; instead, they tend to overestimate their ability to understand new financial products. Finally, and most importantly, most people believe that taking on risk is the main way to make money, and enduring high risk usually brings high rewards. The market must be arranged to make it seem like this, otherwise, people wouldn’t participate in high-risk investments. But the market won’t operate this way forever, otherwise, high-risk investments wouldn’t be high-risk. It is only when taking on risk does not bring the desired result that we realize this investment method truly doesn’t work, and we remember what risk actually is.
summary:
Especially during a bull market, you often hear many people say: “High-risk investments bring higher returns. If you want to make more money, you must take on higher risks.” In fact, it is not possible to generate high returns solely through high-risk investments. Why? The answer is simple: If high-risk investments could reliably create high returns, then their risk wouldn’t be high!

The correct way to put it is that, in order to attract capital, high-risk investments must offer higher potential returns, higher guaranteed returns, or higher expected returns, but this absolutely does not mean that the higher potential return will always be realized.
title: The higher the risk, the greater the uncertainty of return.

content:
It is best to acquire stocks when they are collapsing, especially those that are forced to sell regardless of the price. There is nothing better than this; many of our best trades are made for this very reason. However, we have two observations: You cannot rely solely on buying stocks from forced sellers or selling stocks to forced buyers to make a living, as they won’t always appear in the market—they only emerge during extreme crises and rare bubbles. In our world, buying stocks from forced sellers is the best thing, so the worst thing is becoming a forced seller. This means it is crucial to arrange your finances well; you must ensure that you can hold stocks even in the most difficult times without being forced to sell. This requires both long-term capital and strong psychological fortitude.
During a bubble, investors’ obsession with market momentum will override any concept of value or fair price. Greed (coupled with the internal pain of watching others easily profit) will eliminate the necessary caution.
“Universal Belief in No Risk” is a Rare High Risk In a bull market, especially after the rally has continued for a period, investors often say: “Risk is my friend, because the more risk I take, the higher the reward will be, so please give me more risk.” The reality is that risk tolerance is completely opposite to successful investing. When investors are not afraid of risk, they accept it without demanding compensation… and the compensation for that risk disappears.
A Major Factor in Risk Arises from Believing Risk is Low “No matter what price, I won’t buy it; everyone knows this risk is too high.” I hear many such statements in life, and I have participated in the best investment opportunities because of them…
I firmly believe that investment risk most often occurs where it is least noticed, and vice versa:
When everyone believes that something is high risk, their willingness to buy usually drives the price down to a low-risk level. Universal pessimism makes it the lowest-risk thing because all the optimistic factors in the price have been eliminated. Of course, as the experience of the “Pretty Fifty” investors proves, when everyone believes that something has no risk, the price is driven up to a highly risky level. No risk means there is nothing to fear, and therefore, no reward is provided or demanded for taking that risk—meaning there is no “risk premium.” This turns the most lauded thing into the riskiest thing.

This requires both long-term capital and strong psychological fortitude.
title: Investing is a competition of public sentiment (or: a race for popularity), and the most dangerous thing is buying when the hype is at its peak.

content:
We learned in our introductory course on microeconomics that the demand curve slopes downward to the right: as the price increases, the quantity demanded decreases. In other words, when prices are high, the quantity demanded is relatively low, and when prices are low, the quantity demanded is relatively high. This makes perfect sense, which is why stores perform better when they have special offers. While this operates in many places, it is far from the case in the investment world. Here, many people prefer to buy assets when prices are rising because they feel it confirms their decision; but when prices fall, they are less inclined to buy assets because they start to doubt their initial purchase decision.
No one can comfortably face a loss. Eventually, everyone will wonder: “Maybe I am wrong, the market is right.” The most dangerous time is when they start speculating: “It has fallen too much; I better get rid of it before the stock becomes wallpaper.” This is the mindset that leads to a stock bottoming out… and triggers a frenzy of selling pressure.
In a declining market, there are two basic elements for making a profit: you must have your own view on the intrinsic value, and you must be steadfast. Even if the falling price suggests you are wrong, you must be brave enough to buy. Oh, right, there is a third element: your view must be correct.

Assumptions Behind Efficient Market Theory There are many investors who put in effort to research. They are smart, diligent, objective, active, and well-prepared. They can access available information, and their access channels are generally the same. They can buy, sell, or short (i.e., bet on a decline) all assets. Because of these reasons, the Efficient Market Hypothesis posits that available information is smoothly and effectively integrated into prices, adjusting when prices do not match value, thereby eliminating the discrepancy.
Certain Assets Conform to the Efficient Market, and the Main Types Are Assets that are widely known and tracked by many people; Assets that are socially accepted, non-controversial, or not taboo; Assets that have clear and easy-to-understand advantages, at least superficially; Information related to the asset type and its components is disseminated universally and fairly. Issues in the Above Assumptions Most people are driven by greed, fear, jealousy, or other emotions, which disrupt the possibility of objectivity, allowing obvious errors to take advantage of the situation.
Consider These Questions When thousands of investors rush to buy, willing to drive up the price of cheap assets, why are there still cheap assets? When the return relative to the risk is clearly high, does that mean you might be ignoring some hidden risks? Why are sellers willing to accept a price that allows you to gain excess returns when selling an asset? Do you really know more information about the asset than the seller? If this is such a good deal, why isn’t anyone else rushing to buy it? There is one more thing to remember: The market being efficient today does not mean it will be efficient forever.
Conclusion No market is perfectly efficient or perfectly inefficient; it is merely a matter of degree. I sincerely appreciate the opportunities provided by inefficient markets, but I also respect the concept of efficient markets, and I firmly believe that the mainstream securities market has enough efficiency that trying to find a winner within it is basically a waste of time.
There is a fish in every pond; if you play for forty-five minutes and still don’t know who that fish is, then you are that fish.
summary:
Assumptions Behind Efficient Market Theory

  1. There are many investors who put in effort to research.
  2. They are smart, diligent, objective, active, and well-prepared.
  3. They can access available information, and their access channels are generally the same.
  4. They can buy, sell, or short (i.e., bet on a decline) all assets.

Because of these reasons, the Efficient Market Hypothesis posits that available information is smoothly and effectively integrated into prices, adjusting when prices do not match value, thereby eliminating the discrepancy.
title: Efficient Market and Inefficient Market

Investment Thinking Must Be Different The exceptional insights, intuition, value concepts, and understanding of market psychology required to maintain returns above average. To achieve this, you need second-level thinking.
Doing the right thing might be a necessary condition for successful investing, but it is not a sufficient condition. You must do more things right than others, which means your way of thinking must be different.
What is Second-Level Thinking? First-level thinking says: “This is a good company, so buy this stock!” Second-level thinking says: “This is a good company, but everyone thinks this company is good, so it isn’t a good company. This stock is overvalued, the market price is too high, so sell!” First-level thinking says: “From a forward-looking perspective, economic growth is sluggish and inflation is rising, so sell the holdings!” Second-level thinking says: “The economic outlook is terrible, but everyone is selling stocks out of panic, so you should buy!” First-level thinking says: “I believe this company’s earnings will decline, so sell!” Second-level thinking says: “I believe the decline in this company’s earnings will be less than expected; an unexpected surprise will boost the stock price, so buy!” People Who Practice Second-Level Thinking Consider Many Things What range of outcomes might occur in the future? Which outcome do I believe will occur? How high is the probability that my view is correct? What is the market consensus? How large is the difference between my expectation and the market consensus? How closely does the market price of this asset align with the price believed by the market consensus? And what about my own price? Is the consensus sentiment reflected in the price overly optimistic or pessimistic? If the market consensus proves to be correct, what effect will that have on the asset price? If my expectation is the correct one, what effect will that have? There is a clear and significant difference in the workload between first-level thinking and second-level thinking. The number of people capable of second-level thinking is obviously much smaller than those capable of first-level thinking. First-level thinkers look for simple formulas and easy answers. Second-level thinkers know that successful investing is contrary to simplicity. This doesn’t mean you won’t encounter many people who try to make investing sound simple, I call them “mercenaries.” Securities companies want you to believe that everyone is capable of investing, and that every transaction only costs ten dollars. Fund companies don’t want you to believe that you are capable of investing, but they want you to believe that they are capable of investing, so you will put your money into actively managed funds and pay higher management fees.

  1. First-level thinking says: “This is a good company, so buy this stock!” Second-level thinking says: “This is a good company, but everyone thinks this company is good, so it isn’t a good company. This stock is overvalued, the market price is too high, so sell!”
  2. First-level thinking says: “From a forward-looking perspective, economic growth is sluggish and inflation is rising, so sell the holdings!” Second-level thinking says: “The economic outlook is terrible, but everyone is selling stocks out of panic, so you should buy!”
  3. First-level thinking says: “I believe this company’s earnings will decline, so sell!” Second-level thinking says: “I believe the decline in this company’s earnings will be less than expected; an unexpected surprise will boost the stock price, so buy!”

People Who Practice Second-Level Thinking Consider Many Things

  • What range of outcomes might occur in the future?
  • Which outcome do I believe will occur?
  • How high is the probability that my view is correct?
  • What is the market consensus?
  • How large is the difference between my expectation and the market consensus?
  • How closely does the market price of this asset align with the price believed by the market consensus?
  • And what about my own price?
  • Is the consensus sentiment reflected in the price overly optimistic or pessimistic?
  • If the market consensus proves to be correct, what effect will that have on the asset price?
  • If my expectation is the correct one, what effect will that have?

There is a clear and significant difference in the workload between first-level thinking and second-level thinking. The number of people capable of second-level thinking is obviously much smaller than those capable of first-level thinking. First-level thinkers look for simple formulas and easy answers. Second-level thinkers know that successful investing is contrary to simplicity. This doesn’t mean you won’t encounter many people who try to make investing sound simple, I call them “mercenaries.” Securities companies want you to believe that everyone is capable of investing, and that every transaction only costs ten dollars. Fund companies don’t want you to believe that you are capable of investing, but they want you to believe that they are capable of investing, so you will put your money into actively managed funds and pay higher management fees.

title: Free Temptation: Reconstructing Consumer Value Judgments Through Price Zeroing

content:
When we frantically grab things we don’t need, especially under the temptation of “free,” it may seem irrational, but deep explanations can be found from the perspectives of microeconomics and psychology.
Analysis from the Perspective of Microeconomics: “Zero Price Effect”: This is a very important concept in behavioral economics, specifically used to explain the magic of “free.” Traditional economics suggests that price is merely a quantitative indicator; a price decrease increases demand, but a drop to zero is just a linear extension of increased demand. However, behavioral economics points out that “free” is not just a price of zero; it represents a qualitative leap psychologically, completely changing people’s decision-making patterns.
Reducing Transaction Costs and Psychological Friction: Buying anything requires paying a cost, not just in money, but also in decision-making costs, time costs, and even the psychological “pain of paying.” “Free” completely eliminates these costs and friction. People don’t need to weigh pros and cons or consider if it’s worth it; they just “take” it, greatly reducing the difficulty and psychological threshold of the decision. Risk Aversion and Preference for Certainty: Even for a very small item, if it is “free,” it means “zero risk.” In contrast, buying anything that requires money carries potential risks, such as buying something you dislike or of poor quality. Free items guarantee “at least no loss,” and this certain gain is highly attractive to risk-averse individuals. Value Perception Bias: When the price is zero, people’s perception of an item’s value becomes distorted. We tend to overestimate the value of free items, even if we don’t actually need them. This bias might be because “free” activates the regions in our brain associated with “gaining” and “reward,” making us feel like we got a bargain. Misjudgment of Opportunity Cost: Traditional economics emphasizes opportunity cost—the value of the highest opportunity forgone in order to obtain something. Rational people weigh the benefits of obtaining a free item against the opportunity cost incurred (such as the time spent queuing, the space occupied, etc.). However, under the temptation of “free,” we often underestimate or ignore the opportunity cost.
Neglect of Time Value: To claim a free item, we might need to queue, run errands, or spend extra time. But the halo of “free” often makes us feel that this time expenditure is worthwhile, even ignoring the fact that this time could have been used for something more valuable. Space and Resource Occupation: Free items that are frantically grabbed, if unnecessary, might occupy space in the home or even become trash. But when claiming these free items, we often fail to fully consider these subsequent costs. “Bargain Hunting” Psychology and Transaction Utility: Richard Thaler’s theory of “Transaction Utility” suggests that when people purchase goods, they simultaneously experience two types of utility: Acquisition Utility (satisfaction derived from the actual value of the goods) and Transaction Utility (the feeling derived from the difference between the actual paid price and the psychological reference price).
Super High Transaction Utility from “Free”: When the price is zero, transaction utility reaches its maximum because the actual paid price is far below the psychological reference price (even if the psychological reference price is low). This massive transaction utility makes us feel like we “made a huge profit,” even if the actual value of the goods is low or even negative. The “If You Don’t Take It, You Lose It” Mentality: “Free” reinforces the “if you don’t take it, you lose it” mentality. Even if we don’t need it, the thought that others are grabbing it, or that this opportunity might disappear, makes us more likely to act impulsively to claim it. Analysis from the Perspective of Psychology: Loss Aversion: This is a very important concept in both behavioral economics and psychology. People feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain.
Fear of Missing Out on “Free”: “Free” is often packaged as a limited-time or limited-quantity offer, creating a sense of scarcity and urgency. This atmosphere triggers our loss aversion, making us fear missing out on this “free” opportunity, even if we don’t truly need the items. Weakening of the “Sunk Cost” Effect: For items that require payment, we consider the costs already invested (sunk costs) and hope to maximize their utilization. But for items obtained for free, since no monetary cost was incurred, the sunk cost effect is weaker, making us more likely to claim them impulsively, even if they might eventually be idle or wasted. Social Proof and Conformity: People tend to imitate the behavior of those around them, especially when uncertain or lacking information.
“Herd Behavior” and Group Action: When we see many people frantically grabbing free items, we assume the item must have value, or at least “not be a loss.” This conformity increases the frantic grabbing behavior, forming a “herd effect.” Fear of Exclusion: If everyone goes to claim the free items and we don’t act, we might feel excluded by the group, or that we missed out on some kind of “social opportunity.” Instant Gratification and Impulsivity: Humans are naturally inclined to pursue instant gratification, and “free” perfectly satisfies this psychological need.
Quick Acquisition of Happiness and Satisfaction: The process of claiming free items is simple and fast, immediately providing a sense of happiness and satisfaction from “getting a bargain.” This instant gratification reinforces our impulsive behavior. Weakening of Inhibitory Control: Under the temptation of “free,” we are more likely to relax our guard, reducing our capacity for rational thought and self-control, thus making us more prone to impulsive decisions. Anchoring Effect: When people make decisions, they tend to rely excessively on the first piece of information they receive (the anchor), even if that information is irrelevant to the decision.
“Free” as a Value Anchor: “Free” can serve as a value anchor, making us more likely to accept seemingly “worthwhile” discounts in subsequent consumption decisions, even if those discounts are not truly worthwhile. Contrast Effect and Value Amplification: The existence of free items might make us feel that other items requiring payment are “more expensive,” thereby amplifying the perceived value of the free items. Summary:
Our frantic grabbing of things we fundamentally don’t need, especially under the temptation of “free,” is the result of the combined action of various factors in microeconomics and psychology. “Free” is not just a price of zero; it is a powerful psychological lure that utilizes our Zero Price Effect, Loss Aversion, Social Proof, Instant Gratification, Anchoring Effect, and other psychological mechanisms, leading us to make seemingly irrational decisions driven by impulse.
So, what’s next? We can launch a marketing campaign called “Free Temptation.”

Anchoring Effect Most people only realize what they truly want when they are in a specific situation.
We want to buy a road bike, but don’t know which model, until we see a champion from the Tour de France advertising a certain model and can then clarify what we want to purchase; We want to upgrade our speakers, but don’t know what kind, until we hear a set that sounds better than our current ones and become clear; We don’t even know how to live, until relatives or friends suddenly make us realize that the life they are living is exactly what we aspire to. Everything is relative; that is the key point.
For example, Sam, the TV salesman, plays the same kind of trick on us when grouping the TVs on display: 36-inch Panasonic for $690. 42-inch Toshiba for $850. 50-inch Philips for $1,480.
Which one would you choose? Sam knows very well that customers find it difficult to calculate the value of different TVs. (Who can accurately know that the Panasonic for $690 is a better deal than the Philips for $1,480?) Sam also knows that after giving the customer three choices, most people will choose the one priced at $850. This feeling is like an airplane landing between two runway lights. Can you guess which brand Sam placed in the middle? Not bad, it is the one he wants to sell the most!
One phenomenon is that a high price tag on a main course on a menu can increase a restaurant’s profit—even if no one orders it. Why? Because even though people generally won’t order the most expensive dish on the menu, they are likely to order the second most expensive one. For this purpose, the restaurant introduces a high-priced dish, which tempts customers to order the next most expensive dish (thereby cleverly increasing the profit margin on that dish).

  • We don’t even know how to live, until relatives or friends suddenly make us realize that the life they are living is exactly what we aspire to.

Everything is relative; that is the key point.
