The Only Normal Source of Wealth is Production However, the core reason why the vast majority of people fail is not because they don’t engage in production, nor is it because they never accumulate. Rather, it is because they fail to accumulate for a sufficiently long time, resulting in insufficient capital, and thus they fail to acquire or master true wealth.
Life should be centered around production. Everything else, no matter what it is, must be ranked after it. Nothing is more important than production—at least, until basic necessities are met.
What Exactly Are the Means of Production? Time is the only means of production owned by the proletariat. Time is incompressible, time is uncrossable, and time is always indispensable. You must produce goods and services that can be sold. In other words, someone needs them, or even the entire society needs them, for someone to buy them. Otherwise, how good you feel your creation is is useless. If no one wants it, there is no exchange, and therefore, there is no money. The Fundamental Reason for Life’s Hardship To make money, you must produce, because the only legitimate source of wealth is production; conversely, if you don’t produce, you won’t earn money. Fundamentally, the difference in people’s income primarily stems from the distance from effective production. In other words, the closer you are to production, the more money you earn; or conversely, the farther you are from production, the less money you earn.
The Jobs People Dislike Doing In the past, apprentices mostly focused on the production process; but for today’s workers, the most profitable approach might be to choose the sales process—that is, working in a sales department.
The key here is that sales income has no upper limit. This is unmatched by any other organized form of effective production. The more developed the society, the larger the market, and the richer the variety of goods and services, the more essential sales become to the creators. Therefore, many sales positions have a “performance commission incentive mechanism”—how much you earn depends on your performance. Other positions, such as administration, accounting, and logistics, generally have fixed salaries. So, if you want to earn more, you should prioritize choosing sales.
Absurdly Selling the Means of Production Time is our ultimate means of production. The tragic thing is that 99% of people rely on directly selling their time to earn income. For the vast majority of people, their personal business model throughout their lives is simply selling their time without any processing. Then, they desperately compete at this level, striving to have the highest unit price for their time—that’s all.
The Business Sense Not Taught in School Customer Lifetime Value refers to the profit you can earn from a single customer who buys your product or service throughout their entire life.
The shorter the time cost, the harder it is to make money. For a restaurant, it is actually a quite good business for the average person, and the probability of success is quite high. However, from the perspective of time cost, this business is not the most profitable. It has a certain learning time cost, and while the daily production time cost is not high, it requires continuous production, and every sale incurs a certain time cost.
In comparison,
Creating a book is relatively much more profitable because, although the learning time cost is relatively high (research and preparation), there is also some production time cost (the writing process). But the sales time cost and the reproduction time cost are zero for the author.
Money is a Social Ledger From the essential nature of a social ledger, it can be seen that money is actually the debt of the entire society. It represents what society owes you or the services it owes you. If you are very poor and lack money, it actually represents that you owe society a lot. You have made little contribution to society.
Money can factually store anything, so, of course, money can also be a form of means of production storage.
Money is a means of production. And, it is simultaneously a form of storage.
Money is the most flexible means of production.
Money Has Two Different Uses For most people, money has only one use: consumption. The second, and far more important, use of money is: investment. The desire to invest grows from nothing and becomes increasingly strong. It automatically overwhelms the desire to consume, to the point where, without realizing it, you naturally use more money for investment rather than consumption, unless it is a necessary consumption.
Consumption is naturally joyful because desires are satisfied. But actually, investment is also joyful; it is also a way of satisfying desires, and perhaps it should be even more joyful.
Knowledge is like this, and useful knowledge is even more so. Once you learn it, you cannot forget it. It is difficult for you now to waste money carelessly because you feel it should be used to produce; it is difficult for you to hate the rich because you know they are creditors; it is difficult for you to ignore financial management because you know money is the storage of all things, and your freedom is stored there; it is difficult for you to be content with simply selling your time because you know that is the worst personal business model;
The Fundamental Principle of Producing with Money The essence of investment is actually lending and receiving interest. Even the core of finance is merely interest; and the entire financial market is driven by and exists solely because of interest rates.
Money is actually a form of means of production. Interest is the compensation for the opportunity cost of capital. Just like time, capital is an exclusive resource. This means that its use incurs an opportunity cost.
Regarding Borrowing Money All money lent to relatives and friends is essentially given away; do not expect them to pay it back.
People who know how to produce with money cannot just lend money out casually because their opportunity cost is relatively higher. Upon deeper reflection, many people lend money to others not because they consider themselves generous or benevolent, but because of ignorance or incompetence. The opportunity cost of the money they hold is actually zero, so they don’t care much. Of course, this statement is difficult to hear, but the logic is sound.
Equity is Essentially Equivalent to Debt From the company’s perspective, the company has borrowed a sum of money that never needs to be repaid. From the lender’s perspective, there are suddenly many benefits: higher returns and stronger liquidity. The Fundamental Difference Between Investment and Speculation In the stock market, all investors are traders, but factually, not all traders are investors. Only a tiny minority of traders follow a long-term holding strategy, while the vast majority of traders engage in frequent trading. What is the difference? Only investors consider time as a necessary component of the means of production, whereas the vast majority of traders—let’s call them “speculators”—do not have time in their means of production.
Time is the Only Path to Development. Traders play completely different games in the same arena. Speculators participate in what I believe is the worst kind of limited game, called a “zero-sum game”: the money earned is actually the money lost by others. But investors are different; if they succeed, they earn the “result of development.” What they participate in is actually an “infinite game.”
The Mirror Effect of Investment Risk I am too lazy to even look at financial reports because the best companies are the ones that fake their financial reports the least. I have a background in accounting, so it’s not that I can’t understand financial reports; I just feel that picking stocks by looking at financial reports is like trying to find gold in a pile of garbage. But the problem is, the gold mountain is standing right there, so why bother? The way ordinary people choose stocks is simple: first, try to choose the best goods in life. Then, not only buy the goods, but also buy the stock simultaneously.
The Actual Shape of Individual Time Time is like a container, and inside it are all the people who have lived up to the present, and all the things they have done. Obviously, the size of each person’s time container is different.
This container of time has a starting point and an endpoint, but between the start and the end, time is more like a pipeline than just a straight line. Some people do more things in a unit of time and are more efficient; therefore, this person’s time is different from others’ time—it has a larger diameter, a thicker pipe. Some people do nothing meaningful for a long time; in that period, this person’s time is merely a straight line.
What should we do to make money? Produce, sell, invest. In any case, we absolutely cannot waste this ultimate means of production, time, on things that yield no output.
How to Do More Things After spending time to earn money, we must do more things. More precious than financial freedom is actually time freedom. For those without production capacity, time is merely a ray—instantaneously having no area, long-term having no volume; time is not really a means of production. Therefore, time can only be “bored,” bored to the point of “waste,” and must reach the point of being “killed.” For those with production capacity, time is simply too beautiful; it can be used to create anything, do countless things, and even family affection or love can be “fermented” with time. Furthermore, as production efficiency increases, the possibilities of time become more numerous and greater. This is probably the most exciting reason why we are obsessed with learning and unwilling to learn any skill!
Factors Acting Against Production If you are a producer, or even an effective producer, or even just someone aspiring to be a producer, you must know that there are things that are naturally “anti-production” and absolutely must be avoided. First are drugs and gambling. The ultimate victims of these two things are likely to start innocently, based on the naive idea of “just trying” or “just playing,” holding the侥幸 (lucky chance) mentality that “it won’t happen again.” Little do they know, these two things should not even be touched.
Of course, more common than drugs and gambling is vanity. The definition of vanity can be very clear: money used for consumption was not earned through one’s own production, yet one is not ashamed of it but is proud of it.
Wealth Index = Own Production Income / Own Consumption Expenditure
If a person’s Wealth Index = 1, they are neither poor nor rich; If Wealth Index < 1, they are poor, and the smaller the Wealth Index, the poorer they are; If Wealth Index > 1, they are wealthy, and the larger the Wealth Index, the richer they are. Many so-called wealthy people have the actual dilemma that their consumption expenditure is very high, while their production income is equal to 0, or even less than 0.
Some people genuinely earn money through effective production, but they often fall back into poverty—as the old saying goes, “Seeing the high building, seeing the banquet, seeing the building collapse.” The core reason for falling back into poverty is always the same: the growth rate of consumption expenditure far exceeds the growth rate of production income.
In my words, never increase your consumption level too quickly. In the more than 40 years since the Reform and Opening Up, a large number of so-called “middle classes” have appeared. But once the economy declines, the vast majority of them fall back into poverty overnight. What happened? It’s not that they didn’t earn money; their problem is that they earned money but failed to control their spending. Too many expenditures in life are not necessities but stem from desires from various angles. Desire has no end; if it is not properly controlled, it actually has the power to make anyone fall back into poverty, no matter how strong their production capacity is.
Wealth Gap is Inevitable Every sedan requires at least 4 people to carry it; there must inevitably be poor people, and society needs poor people to function normally.
Basic Principles for Improving Efficiency The act of learning actually includes at least four levels: learning, practicing, applying, and creating. Therefore, just learning without practicing is a waste of time and is the fundamental reason why most people fail to learn. What you learn, you must use; what you learn, you must practice. The process of practice is actually the only way to improve efficiency. Through massive iteration (not just repetition), continuous accumulation, and continuous improvement. Efficiency can never happen overnight, because efficiency must be developed.
Unexpected things will certainly happen in life, and you will encounter bad people and bad events, but these are external factors. Their existence or appearance has already damaged my development; you absolutely cannot let them further devour my ultimate means of production. After all, all my wealth, whether material or spiritual, comes from my time, or more accurately, from the volume of my time. What time do I have to waste? What reason do I have to waste it on them? At all times, focusing on improving efficiency is the main thing.
Summary Wealth comes from production, and it comes from oneself; Time is the ultimate means of production; Money is the storage of all things; Money is the most flexible means of production. In this increasingly better era, as long as you spend your time on self-study, production, sales, and investment, you can earn money, and there are still many things worth doing.
summary:
The Only Normal Source of Wealth is Production

However, the core reason why the vast majority of people fail is not because they don’t engage in production, nor is it because they never accumulate. Rather, it is because they fail to accumulate for a sufficiently long time, resulting in insufficient capital, and thus they fail to acquire or master true wealth.

Life should be centered around production. Everything else, no matter what it is, must be ranked after it. Nothing is more important than production—at least, until basic necessities are met.
title: The sole source of wealth: The value of production and time

Throughout my investment journey, I have come to trust the S&P 500 and consider it the core of my wealth storage. By understanding the US Constitution, the free society, and the powerful military behind it, I believe that the S&P 500 represents the strongest companies and the most stable economy in the world. Here’s why I made this decision and the thinking behind it:
The US Constitution and Free Society are the Strongest Guarantees I firmly believe that the US Constitution and the free society structure are among the most valuable assets in the world. The rule of law and the powerful military, particularly the aircraft carrier, provide a unique guarantee for global investors. If the US Constitution protects investors’ rights and the economy relies on the free market, it will provide a solid foundation for my chosen assets.
Globally, while other countries have excellent companies, they are not protected by a constitution and military power like the US. The US Constitution makes it a special economy, and this guarantee allows American companies to occupy an important position globally. Therefore, I think choosing the S&P 500 is not just choosing a basket of top global companies, but also choosing a system protected by the US Constitution and military power.
S&P 500 Represents the Strongest Global Companies The S&P 500 is not a single “stock” asset; it is a collective symbol of the 500 strongest companies in the world. These companies are leaders in multiple industries and have global competitiveness. Their strength is not only reflected in their market share and financial performance but also in the stable, law-based, free market, and powerful military behind them.
I believe that the 500 companies represented by the S&P 500 not only occupy a leading position in finance and technology globally but also enjoy the protection of the US Constitution and powerful military. This is why I think the S&P 500 has a unique advantage that no other asset can match.
Market Fluctuations and Long-term Beliefs Although the S&P 500 has experienced several market crashes, such as the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, I believe these are just short-term fluctuations. In the long term, the fundamentals of the S&P 500 have not changed; it still represents the strong economic power and corporate competitiveness of the US. Therefore, during market crashes, my decision is not to sell the S&P 500 but to hold it firmly. Even if the market experiences temporary crashes, I do not think any other asset can replace the S&P 500 as a long-term value storage tool.
Many investors choose to sell assets and exchange them for cash during market crashes, but I think the value of cash is far less than the S&P 500. In my view, the S&P 500 is the most valuable asset globally, while cash depreciates over time due to inflation. Therefore, unless it’s for necessary living expenses, I choose to focus my wealth on the S&P 500 and not sell it easily.
Diversification and Risk Management Although I have unwavering trust in the S&P 500, I still maintain a certain level of diversification. In my asset allocation, I invest 90% of my wealth in the S&P 500 and the remaining 10% in the PIMCO Enhanced Short Maturity Active ETF (MINT), which has high liquidity. This configuration not only maintains the growth potential of most of my assets but also provides additional liquidity and risk cushion during market fluctuations.
I chose MINT because it represents low risk and stable returns. This part of my assets can help me maintain a certain level of cash flow during market turbulence, allowing me to respond to unforeseen emergencies or adjustments.
Why Not Diversify into Other Markets or Assets? Many investment experts recommend diversifying investments to reduce risk, such as investing in international markets, gold, or real estate. However, I firmly believe that no country or market can be stronger than the US. The US Constitution and free society are the foundation of my trust, and the US military power and aircraft carriers fleet provide a unique safety guarantee for global investors. In this context, I think the S&P 500 not only represents the top 500 companies in the world but also the strongest economy and military system globally.
Although I understand the importance of diversification, due to my firm trust in the US free society and Constitution, I believe the S&P 500 is the most valuable and worthy long-term holding asset globally. Therefore, I do not tend to diversify my assets into other markets or assets like gold, as they do not have the same guarantees and potential as the S&P 500.
How to Face Uncertainty and Challenges? Although I have deep trust in the S&P 500, I am not complacent about the changes in the global economic situation and political landscape. Although I do not have in-depth knowledge of global geopolitics and international trade conflicts, I remain rational and calm. I cannot predict every market fluctuation, I can rely on long-term investment strategies to cope with these uncertainties.
For me, the core of long-term investment is patience, trust, and determination. Even if the global economy undergoes drastic changes, I will rely on my trust in the S&P 500 and the US system, continue to hold it, and not make emotional decisions due to short-term fluctuations.
Conclusion: Rational Investment, Firm Beliefs Through this period of thinking and investment decision-making, I have established my own investment philosophy: the S&P 500 is not just a stock market index, but a representation of my trust in the US Constitution, free society, and powerful military. I choose to invest most of my wealth in the S&P 500 and maintain a long-term holding strategy because it represents the top companies and the most stable economy globally.
Although I know that global economic and political risks are unavoidable, I believe the S&P 500 is the most worthy long-term holding asset. If the market crashes in the future, I will firmly believe in my decision and not sell easily, but instead, choose to wait patiently for the market to recover.
Epilogue Through in-depth analysis of the logic behind the S&P 500, I am confident in my investment decisions. Long-term market fluctuations cannot shake my trust in the US Constitution and free society, which has given me a more firm belief in my investment path. In my future investment journey, I will continue to adhere to this philosophy, maintain sensitivity to market changes, and continuously increase my knowledge to better cope with potential risks.

content:
Frequency is the Fundamental Factor That Determines Everything In the short term, it is the voting machine; in the long term, it is the weighing machine.
The Higher the Trading Frequency, the Closer the Trade is to a Zero-Sum Game The result of frequent trading is the accumulation of transaction fees, which eventually consumes all your profits and principal.
The shorter the prediction, the closer it is to flipping a coin;
The longer the prediction, the closer it is to true logical deduction…
Therefore, the essence of reducing trading frequency is refusing to flip a coin and insisting on logical deduction.
Risk-Reward Ratio The Risk-Reward Ratio (or Risk-Return Ratio) is an important concept in investment and trading, used to measure the expected return for every unit of risk assumed. It reflects the relationship between the risk and the potential reward of a trading opportunity or investment decision.
Risk-Reward Ratio = Potential Return ÷ Assumed Risk
Potential Return: Refers to the target profit, which is the amount you hope to gain in the trade. For example, if you buy a stock, you expect it to rise to a certain price; the potential return is the difference between that price and the purchase price.
Assumed Risk: Refers to the maximum possible loss you are willing to take, usually determined by the stop-loss price. For example, after buying a stock, you set a stop-loss price; the assumed risk is the difference between the stop-loss price and the purchase price.
Challenges of High Trading Frequency: Frequent trading makes the “Risk-Reward Ratio” of every trade lower. This is because the probability of achieving a massive return in a short period is very low. Even if the market occasionally experiences violent fluctuations (sudden surge or crash), attempting to capture this volatility carries extremely high risk—it is like “picking chestnuts out of the fire”—and easily leads to losses.
The Concept of Risk-Reward Ratio: The Risk-Reward Ratio refers to the potential return that can be brought by a unit of risk. If trading frequently, the potential return of each trade is often not large enough, yet the risk always exists, making it difficult to improve the Risk-Reward Ratio.
The Significance of Actively Reducing Trading Frequency Active vs. Passive:
Active reduction of trading frequency is an action where the trader controls the pace, indicating that the trader is controlling the market rhythm, rather than being dragged along by short-term market fluctuations. Conversely, “unconsciously frequent trading” is a passive reaction driven by market sentiment, usually manifesting as the trader fearing missing out (FOMO) or rushing to chase short-term volatility. How to Improve the Risk-Reward Ratio: Actively reducing trading frequency actually indirectly improves the Risk-Reward Ratio:
Denominator (Risk) remains unchanged: The risk you assume has not increased. Numerator (Return) increases: By reducing frequency, you focus on opportunities with greater potential, increasing the expectation of potential return.

content:
Exhaustion of Entry Capital There are many frustrating laws in the trading market, such as:
Whenever you need money, the market crashes! It might not seem logically supported, so you might temporarily doubt it, but you will definitely experience the magic of this law. For all beginners, this law is almost eternally true: As soon as you buy, it starts to fall; As soon as you sell, it starts to rise… Why does this paradoxical situation occur? Because the fundamental reason for the end of every market trend is the exhaustion of entry capital. In other words, when even the auntie selling tea eggs on the street starts discussing stocks, the market’s “entry capital” is already on the verge of depletion… Think about it, even you, who are completely unrelated to this, know that when it’s time to rush in and make money, the market trend is over, right?
Remedying the Loss Requires a Prerequisite You don’t just have the one sheep that was lost; Besides it, you should have many other sheep; Because you have many sheep, you must have built a “sheep pen” in the past; Therefore, even though you have “lost a sheep,” you still have a chance to “repair the pen”; Therefore, once the “pen” is repaired, you can manage more sheep; Therefore, the loss of one or two sheep initially is negligible to the final result. Therefore, what should the “leek” (retail investor) who “lost the sheep” do? It’s simple: If you have money, slowly add to your position (top up); If you don’t have enough money, desperately make money outside the market. Controlling Position Size You must always reserve a certain proportion or at least a certain quantity of cash—this is non-negotiable, just like a diver needs an oxygen tank. As for what that proportion or quantity should be, there is no fixed theorem; it is entirely up to you to figure it out.
This viewpoint primarily emphasizes the necessity of controlling position size and holding cash. Here is the reasoning and logical analysis:
1. Flexibility of Cash: Dealing with Unknown Risks In the investment market, risk is unavoidable, and market fluctuations can happen at any time. If you invest all your funds in the market without keeping cash reserves, you might find yourself in a passive position when the market experiences a sharp decline or an emergency situation:
Preventing Forced Selling: If the market suddenly drops, holding cash allows you to avoid being forced to sell assets at a low point. Handling Emergencies: Cash is the most liquid asset, which can be used at any time to deal with sudden needs, whether it’s an urgent living expense or an investment opportunity. 2. Cash is the “Oxygen Tank”: Avoiding Full Position Risk Comparing cash to an “oxygen tank” highlights its lifeline significance, especially during extreme market volatility: Buffering Effect: The market environment might be full of pressure, like deep underwater; cash reserves provide you with breathing room during a crisis. Psychological Comfort: Holding a certain amount of cash gives you a greater sense of security during market fluctuations, reducing the possibility of making wrong decisions due to panic. 3. Seizing Opportunities: “Ammunition” During Market Downturns The market is cyclical, and opportunities for undervaluation always arise. If all your funds are invested in the market without keeping cash, you might not be able to utilize the opportunity when it appears:
Averaging Down (Buying on Dip): During market downturns, those with cash can buy quality assets at lower prices. Asset Appreciation Potential: This “ammunition” can help you achieve higher returns when the market recovers. Excellent, Successful Traders Are Ultimately Risk Averse Watch other people taking risks! Sometimes the “correct conclusion” looks so sinister, even shining brightly in the deepest parts. Extreme Fear of Missing Opportunities Fear of Missing Out, abbreviated as FOMO, is also known as Fear of Missing Opportunity.
FOMO, “Extreme Fear of Missing Opportunity.” FOMO is almost the most widespread phenomenon, and the more fundamental it is, the easier it is to be swayed by it. Just look at the slogans used by pyramid schemes or micro-businesses, and you’ll see they are almost always the same:
You missed XXX, and then you missed YYY, and now you want to miss ZZZ?!
The people who lack opportunities the most are the easiest to be incited by such phrases. Calm down and think about it, and you will understand: if you are a person who is not lacking opportunities, even if the price of Bitcoin skyrockets, will you feel anxious because of that fact? No! Because you have other opportunities.
Solitude is the Most Precious Quality of a Successful Trader If you are not good at entertaining yourself, if you do not spend a large amount of time living a serious life, then you cannot reduce your trading frequency, and you will become like a leek staring at the screen all day, keeping your phone within reach even when having sex with your girlfriend—then failure is inevitable.
Experts do not prioritize “correctness,” because anyone can be correct; this is not a particularly difficult thing. The truly difficult thing is that you are not only correct, but you are uniquely correct. Only by being “unconventional and correct” can you generate huge trading value.
Consensus May Create Price (Though Not Necessarily Value)

Risk is a Necessity Many risks are unavoidable. What we should do is assess the risks and then take them. Some risks are not worth taking, no matter how high the potential return is.
Risk Assessment I. What is your ultimate goal? If achieved, what kind of situation will it be? II. How can you achieve your goal with no risk or minimal risk? In other words, what elements can guarantee you reach your target smoothly? III. Are the above no-risk options feasible or desirable? If not, how much risk do you need to take to get what you want?
Hedging (Risk Aversion) A set of strategies that minimizes risk is hedging (or risk aversion). Hedging protects you from losses through balancing measures, seeking equilibrium between risk and safety, much like a woman in a brothel. Alternatively, hedging might be like placing two bets simultaneously, where in a win-only scenario, you ultimately forgo some potential profit to offset potential losses. Another way to reduce risk is through insurance, paying others to bear the downside risk (Note 11). The difference from hedging is that after paying the premium, you retain the full expected benefit. Risk management reduces the probability of the worst-case scenario, but it also brings a disadvantage. Any tool that reduces risk can also be used to increase risk: a safety net can catch you when you fall, but it can also become a trampoline that launches you high up; hedging and insurance are the same. Not only that, reducing risk can allow you to take risks with confidence, ultimately aiming for big gains by taking small risks.
Control Your Emotions, Become the Master of Risk Utilize risk management strategies to reduce your reaction to losses and maintain a consistent attitude when taking risks. This way, you will absolutely not suffer too many losses, and you can remain fully focused on achieving success.

Or anything that contradicts their existing views and conclusions. Therefore, if certain things might be painful, the human brain will start to act and try to deny reality. Psychologist Daniel Kahneman, a Nobel laureate, believes: “People don’t even want to put in the minimal effort to figure out what they did wrong; this is not accidental, but because they simply don’t want to know.”

Everyone Avoids It

We all invent stories for ourselves and evade the facts. Even if you spend a lot of time studying behavioral economics, your skills might only improve slightly. You will always make mistakes. People often ignore or refuse to admit the faults of those they love, and tend to distort the facts to accommodate their loved ones.
title: Even if you don't like reality, you must acknowledge reality.

Even when decision-makers formulate a perfect plan and implement it successfully, unfavorable outcomes can still occur. However, in the long run, it is always wise to focus on following the correct process rather than any specific intermediate result.

content:
Although this book is highly acclaimed in literary circles, from a personal perspective, I do not feel a strong emotional resonance with The Old Man and the Sea. My initial feeling is that the story of this book does not move me. The actions of the old man, Santiago, in my view are reckless and irrational. His persistence and spirit of not giving up, on the contrary, make me feel a sense of aversion. I believe that his battle with the large fish was irrational, as he ignored potential risks and failures, and failed to stop the adventure in time. From the perspective of economics and rational decision-making, this behavior is flawed. His sunk cost is too high, and since there is nothing left to gain, he still insists on going all the way.
Personal Thought Process Initial Feeling: Lack of Resonance When I first started reading The Old Man and the Sea, I did not feel a strong emotional resonance. Santiago’s resilience and tenacity seem to be quite different from my personal life philosophy. Although he did not give up for three days and nights and finally caught the giant fish, I felt doubtful about his stubborn behavior. In my opinion, Santiago’s adventure is full of irrationality; he disregards potential risks and the possibility of failure, ultimately leading to unnecessary losses.
Reflection from an Economic Perspective As someone who emphasizes rational decision-making, my first reaction is that this old man’s behavior has major flaws. In investment and wealth management, cutting losses, identifying risks, and timely strategy adjustment are key to success. Santiago’s behavior undoubtedly contradicts this philosophy; he is too persistent with his “sunk cost” and does not give up at the appropriate moment. Ultimately, even though he won the struggle, the cost he paid due to the attack by sharks was greater than the benefit. This behavior reminds me of some “fighting until the end” practices in life, especially when one is unwilling to correct a wrong decision, which can lead to even greater losses.
Conflict Between Rational Decision-Making and the “Never Give Up” Spirit The “never give up” spirit in The Old Man and the Sea forms a stark contrast with the rational decision-making philosophy that I advocate. In modern society, especially in the investment field, rationality and flexible response are more emphasized than sheer persistence and struggle. I believe that facing challenges, timely admitting mistakes, cutting losses, and adjusting strategies is a more rational and efficient approach. Santiago’s behavior in the book seems somewhat impractical and outdated.
Relationship Between Classic Literature and the Historical Context The Old Man and the Sea was born during the Cold War era of the 1950s. Literature of that era often focused on individual will and the struggle for survival. At that time, many people admired the spirit of unyielding struggle, whereas modern society places more emphasis on rational thinking and effective decision-making. Santiago’s persistence reflects the emphasis on individual spirit and the meaning of struggle during the Cold War, but this may no longer be so suitable for our modern lifestyle and values.
Critical Understanding: The Collision of Classicism and Personal Values Difference Between Personal Understanding and the Classic My low evaluation of The Old Man and the Sea does not mean that I cannot understand its value; rather, it reflects the conflict between my values and the spirit of the book. I do not endorse Santiago’s decision-making style, believing that his stubborn adventure that ultimately resulted in loss is not worthy of praise. As a proponent of rational decision-making, I believe that timely loss cutting and strategy adjustment are the wisest choices. My view does not mean that I lack literary literacy; rather, it is an independent interpretation of the classic work from the perspective of modern society.
Reflection on the Classic Work and Its Value Classic literary works are not perfect; they often challenge our ways of thinking and living. Through critical reading, we can not only understand the work itself but also recognize our own life philosophy and decision-making principles on a deeper level. For me, The Old Man and the Sea is not a simple judgment of “good” or “bad,” but a work that inspires thought and makes me reflect on rational decision-making and life attitude.
Conclusion: Independent Thought and Personal Reading Journey Overall, although I do not feel an emotional resonance with The Old Man and the Sea nor do I endorse its “never give up” spirit, I still believe it is a work worth contemplating. Through the critical reading of this book, I have further solidified my values of rational decision-making and timely loss cutting. The significance of classic literature lies not in whether it conforms to every reader’s philosophy, but in its ability to inspire us to deeply reflect on life, decisions, and principles.
I do not believe that I have “misunderstood” Hemingway, or that my evaluation of the work is flawed. On the contrary, it is precisely this independent thought about classic works that makes my reading journey richer and allows me to gain a deeper understanding of my own life philosophy and decision-making methods.
summary: Although this book is highly acclaimed in literary circles, from a personal perspective, I do not feel a strong emotional resonance with The Old Man and the Sea. My initial feeling is that the story of this book does not move me. The actions of the old man, Santiago, in my view are reckless and irrational. His persistence and spirit of not giving up, on the contrary, make me feel a sense of aversion. I believe that his battle with the large fish was irrational, as he ignored potential risks and failures, and failed to stop the adventure in time. From the perspective of economics and rational decision-making, this behavior is flawed. His sunk cost is too high, and since there is nothing left to gain, he still insists on going all the way.
title: Reading "The Old Man and the Sea": Why I Gave It One Star?

The Difference Between Working and Investing Using money to make money, rather than using time to exchange for money, is the biggest difference between working and investing.
Average Investment Level: Pursuing Relative Victory In the field of investment, achieving absolute victory is not easy, but relative victory is more realistic. Investors who achieve relative victory can become profitable, while those who achieve absolute victory may become masters. However, mastery is not achieved overnight, nor can everyone become a master. Therefore, for ordinary investors, becoming a relative winner should be the main goal.
The Relationship Between Rate of Return and Time Horizon “Investment” refers to putting an individual’s money, time, or energy resources into something expected to yield a profitable or satisfactory return. The return demanded by investors depends on how much investment risk they perceive. If an investment is extremely risky, investors usually expect a higher rate of return.
Time and Liquidity: Key Factors Affecting Returns Risk factors include Time and Liquidity. The longer the time required for an investment, the higher its rate of return should be. The longer others occupy your funds, the greater the possibility of capital loss due to unforeseen events. As an investor, you would want this risk to be compensated.
Furthermore, investors must also consider the liquidity of the funds. Liquidity refers to the ease of investing and withdrawing capital from an asset. When you urgently need money, can you quickly withdraw funds from the invested company? If yes, the investment has high liquidity, or the asset is easily convertible into cash; conversely, it has low liquidity.
Applicability of Installment Payments Due to the existence of uncertain factors, installment payments may be a more suitable choice.
Xiao Chen is deeply in love, but his income is modest, making it difficult to meet his girlfriend Zhenzhen’s material needs. Today is his girlfriend’s 20th birthday, and he must give her a gift no matter what. He gathered a sum of money, bought a gold ring, and wrote on the card:
“Dear Zhenzhen, Happy Birthday! And I wish you happiness on all holidays from today until we get married!”
Stock Market Bottom Fishing: High-Risk Operations Require Caution An old guy, in order to catch the boat, drove to the pier at the fastest speed. When he arrived, he found the boat had already left the shore. He locked the car door and immediately jumped onto the boat at the speed of a hundred-meter sprint, the action flowing seamlessly without any pause. His action startled everyone on the boat, and the captain said in confusion, “Sir… the boat hasn’t even docked yet…”
Bottom Fishing refers to the strategy of buying when the stock price has dropped to its lowest point, especially after a sharp decline in a short period, expecting the price to rebound quickly. Buying the cheapest stock is an opportunity all investors aspire to, and it is the profit model adhered to by value investors. However, there is no clear standard for “cheapest” or “bottom” price. Bottom fishing is often a description of buying at an already occurred low point, but it is difficult to judge what future level will be the true bottom. Furthermore, the rapid decline of some stock prices is not necessarily due to undervaluation, but rather because the company’s fundamentals genuinely have problems. If you buy at this time, the stock price may not only fail to rebound quickly but may also fall further due to unclear fundamentals.
Investment master Peter Lynch once said, “Don’t bottom fish.” This means that if an investor is confident that the company’s fundamentals have no major issues and the stock price has fallen below a reasonable valuation level, they can consider buying without trying to predict the bottom.
Moral Hazard: The Hidden Danger of Selfish Behavior Moral Hazard is not synonymous with moral decay; rather, it refers to actions taken by individuals engaged in economic activities that are detrimental to others while maximizing their own utility. Alternatively, it can be said that when one party in a contract does not fully bear the risk consequences, they will engage in selfish behavior to maximize their own utility. This concept was proposed by Western economists in the 1980s and belongs to the field of economic philosophy.
Moral Hazard manifests in various forms, the most common of which are the following two:
Deliberately Causing Insurance Accidents For example, deliberately causing cargo loss or personal injury to defraud insurance claims. This behavior is becoming increasingly prevalent in our country, especially in life insurance, where cases have occurred of insuring first and then killing the insured person to obtain the insurance payout, posing a threat to social stability.
Deliberately Exaggerating the Degree of Loss When an insurance accident occurs, the insured should immediately notify the insurer and take measures to mitigate the loss. However, some people, in order to defraud more insurance money, do not try their best to mitigate the loss but deliberately exaggerate it. For example, after a ship strikes a reef, the owner bribes the captain to deliberately steer the ship toward the reef, causing severe grounding, which makes fraud easier to achieve.
Productivity Advantage in Competition Whoever has higher productivity is the one who can win in competition. As the saying goes: “I can fight with a broom handle, the problem is, the Northern guys won’t!”
Monetary Attributes of BTC Currency is a specific commodity that fixedly serves as a general equivalent, possessing functions such as a medium of circulation, a means of payment, and a means of store of value. It can satisfy the needs of commodity production and exchange, as well as the need to hold wealth in monetary form.
Never Drink Milk Proactively Given to You by a Miser There is no free lunch in the world. When faced with a sudden windfall, one must remain sober and be less inclined to feel cheap in the face of huge economic benefits.
Supply and Demand are Mutually Causal If there are no good men in the dance hall, will there be good women in the dance hall?
Say’s Law: Supply Creates Demand Say’s Law, also known as the Market Law, states that under normal circumstances, a supply in the market will generate demand for it. Brodeur provides the explanation that any product in the supply market drives the distribution of money during its production process, such as purchasing raw materials, paying freight, and distributing wages. This distributed money will eventually reappear in the form of demand, thus forming a cycle between supply and demand.
Keynesianism: Demand Creates Supply The British economist Keynes proposed a view completely opposite to Say’s Law in the 1930s: that demand can create its own supply. He believed that free mechanisms cannot guarantee stable economic growth and full employment, necessitating stronger government intervention. When demand is insufficient, the government should take measures to stimulate demand, thereby driving economic growth and achieving the goals of full employment and increased supply. This view is known as Keynes’ Law.
Customer Concession Value: The Difference Between Total Value and Total Cost Customer Concession Value refers to the difference between the total customer value and the total customer cost. Total customer value includes product value, service value, personnel value, and image value; while total customer cost covers monetary, time, energy, and mental costs. One way to increase customer concession value is to increase the total value purchased by the customer.
Consumption Imitation Effect: Influence of Surroundings Our consumption expenditure is often influenced by those around us. For example, a young man might not wear the same clothes as his grandfather, but he will wear the same clothes, carry the same shoulder bag, and style the same haircut as his classmates or colleagues. This is the consumption imitation effect.
Snob Effect: The Charm of Scarcity and Expense The Snob Effect refers to consumers preferring goods that only a few people can enjoy or that are unique. The fewer people who own a certain snobbish good, the greater the demand for that good. Fine art, specially designed sports cars, and custom-made clothing are typical snobbish goods. The value consumers derive from them usually stems from the privilege, status, and sense of honor brought about by the fact that “almost no one owns the same thing as me.”
Poor Quality Assets: Worse Than Having Nothing Worse than having nothing are assets that could potentially bring losses at any time. Taking a car as an example, suppose someone gives you a BMW, and the other party pays the down payment; you only need to repay the mortgage monthly. However, you face not only high repayment pressure but also extra expenses such as fuel costs, maintenance fees, and upkeep costs. If you sell the car at this time, the price has often already fallen, and the proceeds are insufficient to repay the loan.
Nowadays, real estate also has a tendency to become a poor quality asset. Negative assets mean not only having nothing but also owing a large debt to the bank. For example, if someone purchases a house with a market price of 1.5 million RMB, and the current market price has fallen to 900,000 RMB, but the mortgage loan and interest owed are as high as 1 million RMB, then the negative asset ratio is 10%.
Structural Unemployment: The Dilemma of Mismatched Supply and Demand An older unmarried man encountered an older unmarried woman in the park and presented the upper couplet: “Having a body of ox strength, but no land to cultivate.” The woman immediately responded with the lower couplet: “Uselessly occupying three feet of good land, with no one to cultivate it.” This is a vivid depiction of structural unemployment: mismatched supply and demand leading to idle resources.

content:
Using new low-interest loans to replace implicit high-interest loans. De facto debt restructuring—there’s nothing new about it; it’s just a routine operation of economic deleveraging.
Four Methods of Deleveraging Debt Restructuring: This refers to changing the terms of existing debt through negotiation, such as extending the repayment period, lowering the interest rate, or partially reducing the principal, in order to alleviate the burden on the debtor. For a nation or large corporation, this may involve complex legal and financial procedures.
Wealth Transfer: This usually refers to transferring wealth from the rich or specific industries to the government or the broader public through tax policies or other means, in order to help repay public debt or support economic recovery. This practice may cause controversy among different social classes.
Spending Cuts: Governments or individuals reduce non-essential expenditures, using the saved funds to repay debt. For governments, this may mean reducing investment in public services and social welfare; for individuals or families, it means reducing daily consumption.
Printing More Currency (Inflation): Although it looks simple on the surface, in reality, this is done by increasing the money supply to dilute the real value of the debt. This method may lead to an increase in the inflation rate, subsequently affecting economic stability and purchasing power.
A Reflection It took me several months to truly realize something so simple and familiar. Perhaps that is the meaning of them inventing new words. To take something you are very familiar with and make it something you don’t understand at all. If you understand a thing very well, then there is no room for maneuver.

content:
In authoritarian regimes, leaders often secure prolonged control through oppressive tactics that prevent opposition from organizing or gaining momentum. From a game theory perspective, this strategy can be understood as a “fear-based stability,” where the cost of opposition is high, and the risk of repression discourages dissenters from taking action.
In such regimes, individuals face a prisoner's dilemma: although collective action could increase the likelihood of challenging the ruler successfully, the first to oppose often suffers severe consequences if others do not join. This creates a situation where everyone prefers to avoid the risk, maintaining a Nash equilibrium in which silence and compliance are rational choices. This mutual inaction leads to a stable yet coercive equilibrium where the authoritarian’s rule remains unchallenged.
However, during extreme conditions—such as famine, economic collapse, or war—this equilibrium may shift. When basic survival is under threat, the difference between acting and not acting diminishes, as both paths may offer similarly low chances of survival. At this point, rebellion equilibrium can emerge, where the collective desperation motivates more individuals to take action despite the risks.
Authoritarian leaders are therefore keenly aware of the need to prevent crises that push citizens into such a rebellion equilibrium. By maintaining a degree of economic stability and suppressing dissent through fear, they preserve their regime’s authority. Nonetheless, game theory illustrates that in the face of overwhelming hardship, even fear-based stability can break, exposing authoritarian rule to the risk of mass uprising.
独裁体制下 独裁者通过高压手段来防止反对派形成威胁，尤其对敢于公开反对的人进行严厉打击。这种严惩措施不仅能立即消除威胁，还能在群体中形成震慑效应，使得潜在的反对者不敢轻举妄动。
同时独裁者禁止人们参与社会组织，防止人们互助，我们可以用囚徒困境来理解它,类似于防止囚徒们合作。
只有当出现饥荒、经济崩溃、战乱等极端情况时，至少一定数量的人生命直接受到威胁，个人的机会成本和风险权衡发生剧变。此时，选择不反抗也意味着几乎没有生存的希望，因此反抗的代价和不反抗的代价趋于一致。
这也是为什么极权政权会极力避免经济崩溃或民生危机，因为这种危机不仅威胁到统治的稳定，也为反抗的发生创造了条件。
summary:
In authoritarian regimes, leaders often secure prolonged control through oppressive tactics that prevent opposition from organizing or gaining momentum. From a game theory perspective, this strategy can be understood as a “fear-based stability,” where the cost of opposition is high, and the risk of repression discourages dissenters from taking action.

In such regimes, individuals face a prisoner's dilemma: although collective action could increase the likelihood of challenging the ruler successfully, the first to oppose often suffers severe consequences if others do not join. This creates a situation where everyone prefers to avoid the risk, maintaining a Nash equilibrium in which silence and compliance are rational choices. This mutual inaction leads to a stable yet coercive equilibrium where the authoritarian’s rule remains unchallenged.
title: Fear-Based Stability and Rebellion Equilibrium

pow(1.5,1/5)-1 如果市场已经下跌了 33% 那么需要上涨 50%才能恢复。如果一年内能恢复的话。 你在-30%处买入会在恢复同样点位时获得 50%的回报 哪怕市场 5 年才恢复，你也可以获得 8%的回报

The other 19 will leave you regretting the purchase at some point in the future. This is why it feels like waiting for a lower price is the right move. Technically, you have a 95% chance of being right.
Why You Shouldn’t Wait Sometimes the lower price never comes, or you have to wait a very long time to see it. Most importantly, you cannot time the market; you don’t know when the price will be better. Because “better” is a relative concept.
Although it feels like we are always at the epicenter of a market crash, the fact is that major crashes are very rare. This is why Average-In has performed poorly for most of history.
Why did “Buy Now” perform so poorly compared to Average-In in August 2008?
Because the US stock market crashed shortly after August 2008. More specifically, if you invested $12,000 in the S&P 500 index at the end of August 2008, by the end of August 2009, you would only have $9,810 (including reinvested dividends), resulting in a total loss of 18.25%.
However, what is truly visible in this chart is not the peak, but the fact that this line is usually below 0%. If the line is below 0%, Average-In performs worse than Buy Now, and when it is above 0%, Average-In performs better than Buy Now.
As you can see, most of the time, Average-In performs worse than Buy Now. This is not just recent bias. If we look at US stock returns since 1920, we find that in every rolling 12-month period, the average performance is 4.5% lower than “Buy Now,” and across all rolling 12-month periods, the average performance is 4.5% lower than “Buy Now.” The chart below illustrates this longer period in the same way as the previous chart.
What About Risk? High returns inevitably bring high risk. Betting on a 4% return with a larger drawdown—is it worth it?

Final Summary When deciding whether to invest all funds now or invest over time, investing now is almost always better. This applies to all asset classes, time periods, and almost all valuation regimes. Generally speaking, the longer you wait to deploy your funds, the worse your situation will be.
The reason I say this is that the only time you can improve by averaging in over time is when the market crashes. However, it is precisely when the market crashes that you are least inclined to invest.
Everyone is frantically selling, and you don’t know how far the market will fall.
It is hard to resist this emotion, which is why many investors cannot continue buying when the market drops, no matter what.
AI Q&A The author’s core view is: Stock markets go up most of the time, so investing early is better than diversifying, because waiting usually means missing out on upward opportunities. Historical data shows that dollar-cost averaging (Average-In) performs worse than lump-sum investing most of the time (76% to 82% of 12-month periods), especially when the market is generally trending upward. Even if lower prices may appear in the short term, the long-term gains from entering the market early are greater.
Rationality of the Author’s Argument Data Support The author provides sufficient historical data to support the argument. Analysis across multiple asset classes and time periods shows that lump-sum buying indeed yields higher average returns. Even during periods of high valuation, lump-sum buying is statistically superior. Theoretical Basis The long-term upward trend of the market indeed supports the logic of investing early. Controlling risk by adjusting asset allocation is a reasonable suggestion. Limitations of the Author’s Argument Psychological Factors Not Fully Considered Investment decisions are not just a matter of math and statistics. The psychological pressure of investing a large sum upfront may lead investors to make poor decisions during market downturns. One of the values of dollar-cost averaging is helping investors build good investment habits and psychological resilience. Differences in Personal Circumstances Different investors have different risk tolerances. The stability of income sources affects the choice of investment strategy. Differences in investment goals and time horizons should also be considered. Complexity of Real-World Situations The real market environment is more complex than historical data. Factors such as macroeconomic environment and policy changes can affect strategy performance. Past performance cannot fully predict the future. Suggested Balanced View Strategy Combination One can consider combining lump-sum buying and dollar-cost averaging. For example, investing a portion of funds upfront while maintaining a regular investment habit. This way, you can gain the advantage of early investment while maintaining investment discipline. Tailored Approach Choose the appropriate strategy based on individual circumstances. Consider your risk tolerance, investment experience, and financial goals. Choosing a method that makes you feel comfortable is more important. Dynamic Adjustment Regularly evaluate and adjust the investment strategy. Make appropriate adjustments based on changes in the market environment and personal circumstances. Maintain flexibility and adaptability. Conclusion The author’s analysis is convincing from a data and theoretical perspective, but investment decisions should not be based solely on historical data. Every investor needs to find a way that suits them, balancing rational analysis with psychological endurance. While dollar-cost averaging might be slightly inferior in terms of pure returns, its value in reducing psychological stress and cultivating investment habits should not be overlooked.

content: The way of navigating life is also the art of adaptation; it cannot be rigidly fixed on one side. Mistakes in the Last Assessment My first speculative attempt, lacked consideration of the factor of project failure (or default). We may need to continuously correct our judgments, because the world is changing. Avoiding Extreme Thinking Being biased toward one side means falling into extreme thinking, believing that a certain strategy or concept can apply forever, or holding an absolute view of certain things. This way of thinking ignores the complexity and diversity of reality. Navigating life and responding to change requires balance; one cannot be too aggressive, nor too conservative. In economic decision-making, behavior biased toward one side may manifest as excessive reliance on a certain policy tool (such as monetary easing or fiscal stimulus), ignoring long-term side effects. Similarly, when individuals invest, if they relentlessly pursue a certain investment model, they may miss other potential opportunities. Winning by Adapting to the Enemy The world is full of uncertainty and variables, whether in politics, economics, or personal life. Facing these changes, rigidly adhering to a fixed strategy or concept will lead to mistakes, or even missed opportunities. Adaptation means adjusting one’s behavior and strategy according to environmental changes, maintaining flexibility and adaptability. The “Winning by Adapting to the Enemy” mentioned in Sun Tzu’s Art of War also emphasizes the importance of responding to change. Whether facing the battlefield or various challenges in life, the ability to adapt to change often determines success or failure. Balance and Moderation The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhong Yong) emphasizes finding balance between extremes. True wisdom lies in knowing when to persist and when to change. This applies to life, career, investment, and politics. Timely adjustments not only avoid the difficulties brought by rigidity but also allow us to better seize new opportunities. “Adaptation” is not blindly following change, but adjusting strategy according to the situation while maintaining core principles. This flexibility allows us to maintain direction while effectively meeting challenges. Open Mindset Responding to change also requires us to maintain an open mindset, always ready to accept new knowledge and new information. Often, success depends on whether we can timely recognize the arrival of change and take corresponding action. Those who always cling to old ideas and are unwilling to accept change are often eliminated during periods of flux. In this age of information explosion, maintaining openness and critical thinking is necessary to avoid being misled and to quickly adapt to new situations and challenges.

More than huge returns, the safety of wealth is more important. Extreme success largely depends on luck. Investing and financial management isn’t entirely luck. It might be a bit like playing cards—there is a considerable element of luck, but there is also a certain level of skill. Personal financial investment is largely related to psychology. Investment behavior is strongly related to a person’s past experiences, because past experiences influence a person’s psychology. Chapter 1: Nobody Truly Loses Their Mind Over Money In the United States, the lowest-income households spend an average of $412 per year on lottery tickets, which is four times the amount spent by high-income households. 40% of Americans cannot pull out even $400 when they desperately need money. This means that those who spend $400 on lottery tickets are basically the people who cannot produce $400 when they need it most. They are betting the $400 that could provide them with security on a chance of winning that is only one in a million.
Few people make financial decisions simply based on electronic reports. Decisions are often made while people are dining or in meetings. In these settings, personal experiences, unique worldviews, subjective self, pride, marketing tactics, and extraordinary incentives all work together to form the context that prompts you to make a decision.
The 401K plan—America’s main retirement system—only appeared in 1978; the Roth IRA was born in 1998. If we consider the latter a person, then he has just reached the age of legal drinking.
Chapter 2: Luck and Risk Nothing is as good or as bad as it appears on the surface.
Scott Galloway, a professor at New York University, put forward an interesting idea, and it is very important to remember this when judging one’s own or others’ success: “Nothing is as good or as bad as it appears on the surface.”
You are more likely to gain valuable insights only when you search for universal patterns of success and failure. The more universal the pattern, the stronger its applicability to your life.

The key to preventing failure is: to do your financial planning so that it doesn’t completely collapse because of one bad investment or an unmet financial goal, ensuring that you can continue moving forward on the investment path until the moment good luck arrives.
Chapter 3: Never Satisfied A considerable portion of readers of this book, at some point in their lives, have earned money or possessed wealth that satisfies all reasonable needs in life and allows them to do many things they want to do.
Chapter 4: The Mystery of Compound Interest Warren Buffett’s net worth is $84.5 billion, of which $84.2 billion was earned after the age of 50, and $81.5 billion was earned after the age of 65—he earned this much starting from the age when he could receive a pension.
If he had started investing around the age of 30 and retired at 60, few people would know about it.
Buffett treated investing as a career from the age of 10. By the age of 30, he had a net worth of $1 million. Considering inflation, this amount is equivalent to $9.3 million today. ￼
If he were just an ordinary person, exploring the world and searching for passion like most people at the age of 10 or 20, how much wealth would he have by the age of 30? Perhaps $25,000?
What if this wealth continued to grow at an excellent annual rate (22%), but he ended his investment career at 60, starting to spend his time playing golf and spoiling his grandchildren?
How much would his wealth be today?
Not $84.5 billion.
But only $11.9 million.
This figure is 99.9% less than his current net worth.
Chapter 5: Wealth vs. Wealth Preservation The fact that “the long-term result is positive, but the short-term process may be terrible” seems counterintuitive at first glance, but many things in life are indeed like this. When everyone reaches the age of 20, the number of synapses in their brain shrinks to half of what it was at age 2, because inefficient and redundant neural connections are cleared, but clearly, a 20-year-old is much smarter than a 2-year-old. Destruction is often a process on the path to progress, but it is also an effective way to refine and select the best.
Imagine you are a parent with X-ray vision, able to see inside your child’s brain. Every morning, you would find that the synapses in your child’s brain have decreased a little more. You would panic and say, “This is wrong, the synapses are decreasing more and more. Something must be wrong; we must do something, we need to see a doctor!” But fortunately, you don’t have X-ray vision. What you see is merely the process of the child’s normal growth.
Economics, markets, and personal careers usually follow a similar path—a process of continuous growth amidst constant losses.
You need short-term vigilance to survive so that you can see the long-term optimistic results.
Chapter 7: Freedom Time freedom is the greatest dividend that wealth can bring you.
The highest form of wealth is when you wake up every morning and can say, “Today, I can do anything I want to do.”
If happiness had a common denominator—a universal source of joy—it would be complete control over life.
The freedom to do what you want, when you want, and for as long as you want, is extremely precious, and this is the greatest dividend that money can bring us.
John D. Rockefeller was one of the most successful businessmen in history. He was also a recluse, spending most of his time alone. He was taciturn, minimizing social interaction, and even if you caught his attention, he would remain silent.
A refinery worker who became one of Rockefeller’s confidants once said, “He let everyone speak, but he himself leaned back in his chair, silent.”
When someone asked him why he remained silent in meetings, Rockefeller often quoted a poem to answer:
A wise old owl lives in an oak tree,
The more it sees, the less it speaks,
The less it speaks, the more it hears,
Why can’t we be like this wise old owl?
Chapter 8: The Luxury Car Paradox There is a paradox here: we all want to use wealth to tell others that we deserve their admiration and respect. But in reality, others often skip the step of admiring you. This is not because they feel your wealth is unworthy of envy, but because they use your wealth as a yardstick to express their own desire to be admired and respected.
You might think you need an expensive car, a luxury watch, and a big house, but I want to tell you that you don’t truly want these things themselves. What you truly want is the respect and envy from others. You think that owning expensive things will make others respect and envy you, but unfortunately, they won’t—especially the people whose respect and envy you desire.
Chapter 9: The Wealth You Cannot See A person’s wealth is invisible because wealth is what remains from income that has not been spent. Wealth exists before you make a purchasing decision. Its value lies in the choices, flexibility, and room for growth it provides you, allowing you to buy more things in the future than you can buy now.
Chapter 10: Saving Money The most effective way to increase wealth is not to increase personal income, but to cultivate your humility.
When you define savings as the difference between your vain self and your income, you can understand why many people with decent incomes find it difficult to save money. This is because they fight daily against the instinct to flaunt themselves and compete with other show-offs.
Chapter 13: Margin of Safety The purpose of the margin of safety is to make predictions unnecessary.
The ability to do what you want, whenever you want, and for as long as you want, is the source of infinite returns on investment.

In a world where everyone changes over time, sunk costs—expenses from past decisions that cannot be recovered—are like a roadblock. They make us prisoners of who we were in the past, preventing us from becoming the different self of the future. This is equivalent to letting a stranger make major life decisions for you.
Chapter 15: There Is No Free Lunch in Life “Any job looks simple to an observer.”
Volatility is akin to a transaction fee, not a penalty. Market returns are never free, and they can never be free. They demand a price from you, just like any other product. You are not forced to pay, just as you are not forced to go to Disneyland. You could go to a local county fair with a $10 ticket, or stay home for free. You might be just as happy, but usually, you get what you pay for. The market is the same. The cost of volatility/uncertainty—the price of obtaining returns—can be called the entry fee, allowing you to gain returns far higher than those offered by low-cost parks like cash and bonds.
Chapter 19: Summary This is because nothing is as good or as bad as it appears on the surface. The world is vast and complex. Luck and risk truly exist.
The less vanity, the more wealth. How much money you can save depends on the gap between your need for self-expression and your income, and wealth precisely exists in the unseen places.
Some Thoughts How to Achieve Financial Freedom by Trading Stocks Buffett’s True Secret to Success Buffett does not borrow heavily. Buffett has survived 14 economic downturns, but none of them made him panic-sell stocks. Buffett never tarnishes his business reputation. Buffett never clings to one strategy, one worldview, or one trend; he is always learning and never goes all-in on one thing. Buffett does not govern the company using other people’s money. Buffett has not exhausted himself, nor has he quit or retired. Buffett repeatedly emphasizes the so-called “margin of safety.” His strategy requires that even during a massive bull market, you must always hold some cash. When everyone else is fully invested and earning a 9% return, your cash might only yield 1% return. This feeling is difficult, but you must endure this discomfort to ensure that during a bear market, you still have money and are not forced to sell stocks.
Making Money is One Thing, Preserving Wealth is Another. It is foolish to take risks with the money you have and need in order to make money you don’t have and don’t need. To make money they didn’t have, and didn’t need the risk what they did have and did need and that’s foolish. It is reasonable to invest a small portion of income without affecting the quality of life. But people must be careful of the “Never Enough” impulse and should not take excessive risks (leveraging investments, shorting stocks, stepping over legal lines, etc.) to pursue more wealth; instead, they should focus on preserving wealth and slowly increasing it through the power of compound interest for sustainable development.
Taking Risks Can Make You Money, But It Can Also Make You Lose It. Making money relies on luck, optimism, and willingness to take risks. Preserving money requires avoiding risks, extreme humility, and having fear in your heart. The Straight-A Student vs. The Treasure Hunter The Straight-A Student This mindset is like those good students in school who hope to get good grades in every subject and fear having any weak points. If this person does ten things, they expect to do at least nine well, and they will apologize for the one that wasn’t done well.
But the straight-A student mindset is actually an employee mindset. Everything you do is pre-arranged and must be done. So, if you don’t know what to do right now, or what the consequences of each action will be. If you are an entrepreneur, an investor, or a leader, this employee mindset won’t work. You have to select a few things from a large pile of potentially beneficial things.
The Treasure Hunter Those who invest know that investment portfolios have a strong tail effect. Often, most of the projects you invest in are not successful, but a few will be extremely successful, and almost all of your returns come from those extremely successful projects. This effect is the “80/20 Rule” in investing. Moreover, this “investment” is broad, not limited to stock trading.
The key to the treasure hunter mindset is casting a wide net. If you estimate there might be gems in this mine, can you say you only explored the spot with gems? Can you say you only bought the pit with gems? You must control the entire large area. Football schools, celebrity agencies, copyright representation, IP adaptation—all follow this mindset.
We live in a world where “good things” are distributed very unevenly.
In your lifetime, perhaps only a few books will have the deepest impact on you. Perhaps only one or two skills will determine your future. Perhaps only a few events will change your destiny. Perhaps there are only a few people who are most important to you. You must cast a wide net, try many things, and expand your search range, not fearing the waste of time and money, to ensure you find the best few.
If you only want to do the right things, the things proven by history, your path will become narrower and narrower.
Why Ambitious People Live in Disappointment of Themselves These are truly “gray” days. You didn’t sell at the last peak, and you don’t know when the next peak will come; the current point only brings you disappointment. These are the days when a top student scores 97 points.
Investing is an activity that everyone can participate in, and it provides direct feedback on your decisions. In particular, investing shows whether you can face the real world.
So, if you are an ambitious person, your days are spent pursuing occasional satisfaction amidst disappointment.

to leave this world a little better than we found it.
The Money Trap: The Old Road Map for Money We Aren’t Making a Living, We’re Making a Dying
For so many working people, however, from people who love their work to those who barely tolerate their jobs, there seems to be no real choice between their money and their lives. What they do for money dominates their waking hours, and life is what can be fit into the scant remaining time.
Money Ain’t What It Used to Be—and Never Was Money is something you trade your life energy for. You sell your time for money. It doesn’t matter that Ned over there sells his time for a hundred dollars and you sell yours for twenty dollars an hour. Ned’s money is irrelevant to you. The only real asset you have is your time. The hours of your life.
Money is life energy Money is also like water—it flows, and as it flows, it nourishes life.
Knowing money is life energy allows you to maximize and optimize your most precious resource: your time; your life.
Now that you know that money is something you trade life energy for, you have the opportunity to set new priorities for your use of that valuable commodity. After all, is there any “thing” more vital to you than your life energy?
Men do not desire to be rich, only to be richer than other men. Enough for you may be different from enough for your neighbor—but it will be a figure that is real for you and within your reach.
When you are financially independent, the way money functions in your life is determined by you, not by your circumstances.
当你经济独立时，金钱在你生活中的运作方式是由你决定的，而不是由你的环境决定的。
Establish (accurately and honestly) how much money you are trading your life energy for, and discover your real hourly wage. Learn about your money behavior by keeping track of every cent that comes into and goes out of your life. Where Is It All Going? budget can be an amazing tool to lasso your wild spending and get it to behave.
You need to identify and follow internal signals, not external admonishments or habitual desires. You need to observe and adjust your patterns of spending over the long term, not what you spend over the short term.
Where to Stash Your Cash for Long-Term Financial Freedom CHECKLIST OF THINGS TO CONSIDER WHEN INVESTING Is this investment in line with my values?
Is this investment in line with my tolerance for risk?
Does this provide overall diversification for my investments?
Does this provide the current and future income I need?
How easily can I liquidate (sell out of) all or part of this investment?
What sales charges or penalties (if any) will I incur in getting into or out of this investment?
What are the federal, state, and local tax implications of this investment for me?
(Is it tax efficient for my income bracket or situation?)
What are you putting in place now to keep you afloat as you age?
In a pinch, what could you do to make extra money?
Whom or what would you trust to help you invest your money?
What’s been your experience to date with investing?
What are your hopes?
What values and beliefs do you bring to investing?
What is your risk tolerance—in money and life?
What does Financial Independence mean to you?
summary:
In fact, a healthy relationship with money is most often just a by-product of living a happy, healthy life.

Endless desire is one of the pitfalls of human nature, and one of the first things you need to cure if you want to get ahead more quickly.

What will you do when you no longer have to work for money?

to leave this world a little better than we found it.
title: Your Money or Your Life
